items.title: Eckert 1864: two telegrams, Fox to Butler and Meigs to Butler, 21-22 Apr 1864
items.content: Fox asks Butler to block the channel at Roanoke Island so the ram cannot get into Pamlico Sound, while camels are built to lift the monitor Tecumseh over the 8-foot bar at Hatteras to protect everything south of Roanoke Island. The next morning Meigs tells Butler that 4,000 men, not three regiments, are waiting in Washington for Fort Monroe, that Butler holds all the transportation and should send it up for them, and that 1,000 cavalry horses are ready at the cavalry depot.
items.context: The CSS Albemarle had just helped the Confederates retake Plymouth, NC (20 Apr 1864), and the Navy feared the ram would break out into the Sounds. Fox, Assistant Secretary of the Navy, turned to Butler, whose department covered North Carolina. In the same days Butler was assembling the Army of the James at Fort Monroe for the Bermuda Hundred landing of 5 May, and Meigs was shipping Tenth Corps detachments and horses to him.
items.what_is_added: Both telegrams in their own words. Their substance is already in print: Butler's reply (OR I/33 p.279), Fox's parallel telegram to Ericsson about the camels ten minutes earlier (ORN I/9 p.667), Butler's question that E5 answers (Butler Corr. IV p.112) and Halleck's 1,000 horses (OR I/33 pp.938, 940). Most of the words have been in clear on the Huntington page since 2018 (about 53 of 63 and 40 of 60). Ours is the code words: Roanoke Island, 8 feet, 'South', the signatures, and Meigs's figures. The two figures not in print are 4,000 men instead of 3 regiments and the horses waiting at the cavalry depot, along with 'you have all the transportation'.
items.why_tier: These are the actual texts behind an exchange whose decisions (obstruct the channel, camels for the Tecumseh, horses and men to Butler) are already documented. Meigs's 4,000-men figure sharpens the account a little but changes nothing.
items.caveats: The strongest item in the group (N4, D4, two ledger copies, a blind second reader agrees on 96%). Unpublished copies (NARA M504, Meigs letterbooks) are unread. E5's 10.45 AM header disagrees with its 10.30 time word. From general knowledge, not checked: the camels plan was not carried out, and the Tecumseh went to the James and then to Mobile Bay.
items.checked_externally: Repo only for the print record (AUDIT.md sections 5-6, 'N4 set', G3 check V1-G3A). The Plymouth/Albemarle and Bermuda Hundred context is general knowledge; no new search.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Augur to Ingalls, 9 Mar 1864, Grant coming down to the Army of the Potomac tomorrow (N2-AJ)
items.content: At midnight on 9 March 1864 Augur tells Brig. Gen. Ingalls (chief quartermaster, Army of the Potomac) that Lieutenant-General Grant will come down to the Army of the Potomac the next day.
items.context: Grant received his lieutenant-general's commission from Lincoln on 9 March 1864 and visited Meade's headquarters on 10 March. Both the visit and its date are in print (Humphreys's circular and Stanton to Burnside, 'General Grant has gone to the front', OR I/33 pp.663-664). Augur commanded the Department of Washington.
items.what_is_added: Only the wording of a one-line advance notice. The public Huntington transcription had 'will be down to the ... to more row'; the reading supplies Grant, Army of the Potomac, Ingalls and Augur. The G3 check found that it adds no fact not already printed.
items.why_tier: It is a staff heads-up about a famous and well-documented event, with no new detail.
items.caveats: N3 only because Augur's own telegram book (NARA RG 393) is unread. D4. The header was corrected from 'noon' to 'midnight'.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (D12-VP sections 3-4, D4-V2AJ, V1-G3A). The commission date is general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Judge Advocate Turner, 10 Oct 1864, Jewett and Siebert from Richmond; Gemmell in the Old Capitol (E27)
items.content: Judge Advocate L. C. Turner tells 'beverage' in New York that two men, Jewett and Siebert, came from Richmond last week, one going to 'harem' and the other to New York, and are supposed to be Rebel agents. James Gemmell, who crossed the Potomac with them, is now in the Old Capitol, and a Miss Gardner who travelled with them, who had been teaching in the South, was going to Norwich, Connecticut.
items.context: Levi C. Turner, associate judge advocate at Washington, worked with L. C. Baker on the War Department's investigations of political prisoners and suspected disloyal persons, many of whom were held in the Old Capitol Prison. By October 1864 the department was watching traffic from Richmond into the North and tipping off New York (here through the operator Horner).
items.what_is_added: The names Jewett, Siebert, Gemmell and Gardner are in clear on the ledger page. The reading adds what the public transcription hides: that the men came from Richmond, that they are Rebel agents, that one was bound for New York, that Gemmell crossed the Potomac, and Connecticut and 'the South'. Two audits found no print, press report or prison record naming any of the four.
items.why_tier: It names suspected agents and a prisoner, and would interest a historian of Union counter-intelligence or the Old Capitol. But none of the four is identified, and the tip itself is ordinary surveillance traffic.
items.caveats: D3 (93%). The place word 'Grunt' is M (the book gives Warrenton, but the telegram was sent from Washington), and the addressee 'beverage' is an unread name code. 'harem' is left plain; Harlem is my guess, not the repo's reading. NARA M797 (the Turner-Baker case files, the likeliest place these people appear) is unread.
items.checked_externally: One web search for 'Gemmell' 'Old Capitol' 1864: no hit. Otherwise repo only (LS-V1, AUD2-LS-B).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Seward to Murray and Harrington to Barney, 13 Aug 1864, detain the schooner Princess (E40)
items.content: Seward orders Robert Murray, U.S. Marshal at New York, to detain the Princess and her cargo for further orders. Acting Secretary of the Treasury George Harrington orders Collector Hiram Barney to detain the schooner Princess and, with the marshal's aid, examine her cargo. A tail note says to let 'the Boston message' go forward once these two have had time to take effect.
items.context: On 10-14 Aug 1864 the State and War Departments moved against the network of Alexander Keith Jr., the Confederate agent at Halifax. The related ledger items E38 and E39 order the seizure of his remittances to Boston and New York. Huntington sibling 9820 (13 Aug) concerns machinery being supplied for Keith through Montreal, and 9047 (14 Aug) asks Murray whether the Princess 'was detained as directed yesterday or whether she got off'. Keith later became notorious as the 'Dynamite Fiend' of the 1875 Bremerhaven explosion (general knowledge).
items.what_is_added: The joint State/Treasury order to stop and search a named schooner. Two audits searched the 1864 press (NYT and Chronicling America), the OR and Foreign Relations and found no report of the detention. The code words supply New York, the officers' titles and the signatures.
items.why_tier: It is a concrete step in a little-documented operation against a Confederate supply channel. Taken alone, though, it is a one-line detention order: the cargo, the outcome and even the Princess's link to Keith are not stated in it.
items.caveats: D3 (92%). One code word ('nick') is unread, and the Seward signature carries a [?]. The tie to Keith is inferred from adjacent telegrams, not stated, and the outcome is unknown. Unread: NARA RG 59, RG 36 (NY Collector), RG 21, and the Seward Papers.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (LS-V3, AUD2-LS-C, including the Huntington siblings 9820 and 9047). Keith's later notoriety is general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Rucker to Newport, Baltimore, 29 Nov 1864, every available steamer and propeller (E45)
items.content: Brig. Gen. D. H. Rucker, quartermaster at Washington, tells Colonel Newport, chief quartermaster at Baltimore, to send to Washington at once every available steamer and propeller in service at his post that can be spared, and to find out and report the names of those he sends.
items.context: On 28 Nov 1864 Grant asked Sheridan for the Sixth Corps, and Sheridan said he would start it by divisions on the 30th. At 1 p.m. on 29 Nov Halleck pressed Sheridan, 'Please answer immediately, as I have ordered steamers here' (OR I/43 pt 2 p.695). The corps went by rail to Washington and then by water to City Point in early December. E45, sent that morning at 10.45-11 AM, is very probably that steamer order.
items.what_is_added: The working order behind Halleck's printed remark: Baltimore's steamers were called to Washington the morning of 29 Nov, before Sheridan confirmed the corps would leave. The telegram's text was not located in print or in the press.
items.why_tier: It is logistics that confirms and slightly sharpens the timing of a known troop movement.
items.caveats: D3 (100% of code words H). The time word gives 11 AM against the 10.45 header. The link to the Sixth Corps is my inference from OR I/43 pt 2 pp.684-695; the two audits did not record Halleck's 29 Nov remark, and a verifier may want to weigh it ('context in print, text not', the E47 shape). The reading's 'that Canby spared' is probably the clerk's phonetic 'can be spared', not General Canby. A twin message to City Point on the same page is unread.
items.checked_externally: Grepped the repo's cached OR I/43 pt 2 full text (sources/ia-fulltext/print-check/warofrebellion432unit) for 26-30 Nov 1864: Grant 28 Nov 5.30 p.m., Sheridan 28 Nov 9.30 p.m., Halleck 29 Nov 1 p.m. on p.695. Also one web search on the Sixth Corps' December 1864 move.

items.title: Eckert 1864: W. H. Whiton to Adna Anderson, Government Railroads, Nashville, 21 Oct 1864, accept the inspector-generalship (E51)
items.content: W. H. Whiton urges Adna Anderson of the Government Railroads at Nashville to accept the proposed inspector-generalship promptly and without question, saying it is all right, carries greatly increased powers and better advantages, and that he will like it.
items.context: Adna Anderson was general superintendent of the U.S. Military Railroads in the Military Division of the Mississippi, the line supplying Sherman's and Thomas's armies. The Nashville Daily Union of 9 Nov 1864 reported his appointment as General Inspector of U.S. Military Railroads, with E. L. Wentz succeeding him. His ASCE memoir (1889) and McCallum's report give the same change.
items.what_is_added: Only the private urging and Whiton's reasons. The appointment itself is in print.
items.why_tier: It is a personnel nudge whose outcome is already documented.
items.caveats: D3. Whiton is not identified in the audits. Grant Papers vol. 13 and the USMRR records are unread.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (LS-V4, AUD2-LS-E).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Washington (General-in-Chief code word) to Sherman, Nashville, 27 Apr 1864, the 11th Michigan Cavalry of no use at Lexington (E59)
items.content: Washington tells Sherman at Nashville that the Cavalry Bureau reports the 11th Michigan Cavalry is of no use at Lexington, that its efficiency is being impaired, and that it ought to be sent to the field.
items.context: A week before the Atlanta campaign opened, the regiment was at Lexington, Kentucky, under Hobson (OR I/32 pt 3). The signature is the book's 'General-in-Chief' word. E6, sent the day before with the same signature, is printed as Halleck's (OR I/32 pt 3 p.498), so this is probably Halleck as chief of staff (inference).
items.what_is_added: One routine recommendation about one regiment, not located in print.
items.why_tier: It is administrative cavalry traffic with no bearing on any known decision.
items.caveats: D3 (92%). From general knowledge, not checked: the 11th Michigan Cavalry stayed in Kentucky through 1864 (Cynthiana, Saltville), so the suggestion apparently did not send it to Sherman's field army. Sherman's printed correspondence was searched only by phrase.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (LS-V5, AUD2-LS-F).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Sheridan, 12 Dec 1864, a revoked assignment and a chief quartermaster for his army (N2-BK)
items.content: Meigs tells Sheridan that his dispatch was received and the Secretary of War has been asked to revoke an assignment, which had been made mainly because the officer was already acting in that capacity under Sheridan's orders. He asks whether Sheridan's army needs a chief quartermaster and, if so, who is most capable and most worthy.
items.context: December 1864, Sheridan's Middle Military Division after Cedar Creek. From general knowledge, not checked here: his chief quartermaster, Lt. Col. C. W. Tolles, had been mortally wounded by guerrillas in October 1864, which would explain the question.
items.what_is_added: The wording of a staffing exchange. Neither the officer nor the assignment is named.
items.why_tier: It is quartermaster personnel business with no named persons and no consequence traced.
items.caveats: D2 (91%; 8 H, 2 C, 1 I). The Grant Papers vol. 13 for December 1864 are unread (the named next step).
items.checked_externally: Repo only (LS-V6, AUD2-LS-G). The Tolles point is general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Stanton via Capt. Bruch, Louisville, to Burbridge, 7 Aug 1864, hear Surgeon Ferry's statement and send him to Washington under guard (E68)
items.content: Through Captain Bruch at Louisville, Stanton directs General Burbridge to see Surgeon Ferry in person and hear his statement. If Burbridge finds the communication trustworthy and important, he is to send its substance by cipher telegraph; if a personal interview with Stanton seems important, he is to send Ferry to Washington under an adequate guard that will see he does not escape.
items.context: In August 1864 Burbridge commanded the District of Kentucky under martial law. That summer the War Department was pursuing disloyalty and conspiracy cases in Kentucky and the Northwest. The order shows the Secretary of War personally handling an informant's statement, but the text does not say what the statement concerned.
items.what_is_added: The existence of the Surgeon Ferry matter and Stanton's handling of it. Two audits found Ferry in none of OR I/38 pt 5, I/39 pt 2, II/7 or the 1864 press.
items.why_tier: It is a genuine lead, a sensitive statement important enough for Stanton's own order. Without knowing who Ferry was or what he said, though, it adds a thread rather than a fact about any known episode.
items.caveats: D3 (89%). 'Jones' ('insert Jones cipher') is M and 'platation' (communication) is I. Ferry is unidentified, and any tie to the conspiracy investigations is speculation. OR ser. III vols 4-5 and NARA RG 107 are unread.
items.checked_externally: One web search for 'Surgeon Ferry' 1864 with Burbridge/Kentucky/Louisville: no hit. Otherwise repo only (LS-V7, AUD2-LS-H).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Van Vliet, New York, 22 Apr 1864 10 PM, complete the supply of tugs, ferry boats, barges and schooners for Fort Monroe and Washington (O9-BB)
items.content: At 10 PM on 22 Apr 1864 Meigs tells Major Van Vliet, quartermaster at New York, to complete the supply of tugs, ferry boats, barges and schooners for both Fort Monroe and Washington, says there will be much material to move and that steamers enough to move the troops are now engaged, and orders him to devote himself to hastening the vessels to their ports, since delay would be most injurious.
items.context: This is the same week as E5: the water transport for Butler's Army of the James and the Bermuda Hundred landing of 5 May 1864 was being assembled. Meigs's earlier order of 20 Apr to Van Vliet (Huntington 8939, mostly in clear) splits tugs between Washington and Fort Monroe.
items.what_is_added: Three code words only: Fort Monroe, Washington and Troops. The rest of the order has been in clear in the Huntington's public transcription since 2015.
items.why_tier: It is logistics, mostly already public, with no new figure or decision.
items.caveats: Weak N3 (the audit notes a third audit could reasonably call it N2). 'Surgery' is M. The 13 Van Vliet press pages of that week are unread.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (LS3-V18a, AUD2-LS3-A, V1-G3B).

items.title: Eckert 1864: C. A. Dana to Baltimore, 5 Nov 1864 11 PM, Colonel William Hamilton reported as a Rebel agent in Baltimore (E96)
items.content: At 11 PM on 5 Nov 1864 Assistant Secretary of War Dana telegraphs Baltimore that a Colonel William Hamilton is reported, on what seems trustworthy evidence, as a Rebel agent in Baltimore, and warns that if several persons answer to the name, care must be taken to get the right one.
items.context: This was three days before the presidential election of 8 Nov 1864. That Saturday Dana sent a set of orders for arrests on Monday morning, 7 Nov, of named Rebel agents in Cincinnati, New York and Memphis; the siblings are in clear on the Huntington pages. The same weekend saw the Camp Douglas arrests in Chicago (night of 6-7 Nov), amid fears of plots against the election. E96 appears to be the Baltimore part of that sweep, and a follow-up of 7 Nov (E52) chases a 'Dr Hamilton' seen at Elmira.
items.what_is_added: The name 'William Hamilton' was public in clear. The code words supply 'Colonel', 'reported', 'Rebel', 'Baltimore', 'right' and Dana's signature. Per the audits, the 5 Nov arrest set is not in the Official Records.
items.why_tier: It adds a Baltimore target to a little-printed pre-election security sweep, but the man is unidentified and the outcome unknown.
items.caveats: Weak N3, D2 (86%; 'William' and 'persons' are M as numeral-row words). The press of the day was unreachable (loc.gov Cloudflare), and the Dana papers and RG 107 are unread. Whether Dr Hamilton (E52) is the same man is unknown.
items.checked_externally: One web search on the 5 Nov 1864 arrests and the Camp Douglas plot, which confirmed the Chicago arrests of 6-7 Nov. Otherwise repo (FV-LS4-R1b, V1-LS4B).

items.title: Eckert 1864: to Col. Bradley, chief quartermaster, City Point, 18 Dec 1864, boats in the James for Sherman's transports (N2-CJ)
items.content: On 18 Dec 1864 Col. Bradley, chief quartermaster at City Point, is told that the orders first given about the transports for Sherman will be carried out, and that those of the named boats now in the James are to be sent off to their destination without delay.
items.context: Sherman had just reached the coast at Savannah. Meigs and Grant's printed exchange of 19 Dec (OR I/44 p.755) tells the story: Hilton Head had called for light steamers for Sherman on the Ogeechee, and Grant had briefly forbidden vessels going to Savannah, thinking they were to move Sherman's army north. Grant then 'soon learned the facts, and directed General Ingalls to go on'. This telegram is that go-ahead.
items.what_is_added: The operative order itself. The episode and its resolution are already printed.
items.why_tier: It confirms a small, already-explained mix-up over transports.
items.caveats: Weak N3, D2 (87.5%). The frame is clear in the public transcription, so only two content code words (Sherman, James) are ours. The signature 'Rue Two In galls' is M; the image suggests 'Rue Fus' (Rufus Ingalls).
items.checked_externally: Repo only (FV-LS4-R2b, AUD2-LS4C, quoting OR I/44 p.755).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster General via Capt. Bruch to Brig. Gen. Allen, Louisville, 12 Dec 1864 2 PM, should the Military Railroads take the Louisville and Nashville (E146)
items.content: The Quartermaster General tells Brig. Gen. Allen, chief quartermaster at Louisville, that General Donaldson recommends the manager of the U.S. Military Railroads be instructed to take immediate possession of the Louisville and Nashville Railroad as vitally necessary to sustain the army. He asks whether Allen concurs, or whether placing some military-railroad rolling stock on the road would suffice, and whether the L&N company could not do all that is possible without the interruption of changing hands. A partly unread closing seems to say government freight and travel should have preference, and perhaps exclusive use of the road.
items.context: Four days before the Battle of Nashville (15-16 Dec 1864), Hood's army stood before Nashville and the L&N was Thomas's rail link to Louisville and the North. The L&N, under its president James Guthrie, stayed a privately run company through the war and resisted federal control. Donaldson was chief quartermaster at Nashville; Allen was chief quartermaster of the Mississippi Valley at Louisville.
items.what_is_added: The public Huntington frame already shows Donaldson's recommendation to 'take immediate possession' of something. The reading names the road (Louisville and Nashville Railroad), the army and Louisville, and identifies the sender as the Quartermaster General. It also brings out Meigs's apparent preference to leave the company running. Neither audit found this in OR I/45 pt 2.
items.why_tier: It records a proposal at the crisis of the Nashville campaign to seize a major private railroad, and the Quartermaster General's hesitation. A historian of the L&N's wartime relations with the government, or of USMRR policy, would want to cite it. This is provisional: it drops to useful-detail if the L&N histories (Cotterill 1924, Klein 1972, Dan Lee 2011) or Quartermaster records already discuss Donaldson's December recommendation.
items.caveats: Weak N3, D2 (26 of 26 read code words H, but 'Tartan' and 'Stan' are unread and the closing sentence is garbled). The frame is public, so the idea of seizing 'something' was visible to any reader of the transcription. The L&N secondary literature, the QMG and USMRR records, and Allen's or Donaldson's replies are unread. I did not establish whether the proposal is already known.
items.checked_externally: Two web searches on the L&N and a December 1864 seizure: no source on Donaldson's recommendation found. Guthrie's resistance to federal control is confirmed (Wikipedia), and Lee's 2011 book exists but its contents were not read. One Internet Archive full-text query found nothing relevant. Google Books was unavailable (daily quota exhausted, HTTP 429).

items.title: Eckert 1864 (Fort Monroe ledger): Butler's HQ to Fort Monroe, 1 Nov 1864 12.30, the best five batteries of the Army of the James (E162)
items.content: On 1 Nov 1864 Lt. Col. Howard's office (signed R. O'Brien) at Butler's headquarters answers Captain Martin at Fort Monroe with a list of the best five batteries of the Army of the James. The Napoleon batteries listed are Battery M, 1st U.S. Artillery and Battery E, 3rd U.S. Artillery; the others are the 17th New York (3-inch), Battery D, 1st U.S. Artillery and Battery F, 5th U.S. Artillery.
items.context: Butler was sent to New York City with troops to keep order at the presidential election of 8 Nov 1864. He asked for 'at least two batteries of Napoleons' (Butler to Grant, 2 Nov, OR I/42 pt 3 p.489), and Battery M, 1st U.S. and the 4th New Jersey went (OR I/42 pt 3 p.490; Hawley, OR I/43 pt 2 p.559). Martin's request for the list is in clear on the same ledger page.
items.what_is_added: The staff's short list of the five batteries considered best. Which batteries actually went is already in print.
items.why_tier: It is a staff list whose practical outcome is documented; at most a footnote to Butler's New York election command.
items.caveats: D3 (97%). The ledger itself disagrees on the 17th New York's guns ('3 inch' here, 'Napoleons' in E160 the next day). Butler's Book was read by snippet only, and Butler's letterbooks are unread.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (FV-FM1, AUD2-LEDGER-3).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster-General to Canby, 11 June 1864, the Vicksburg and Shreveport gauge (N2-M)
items.content: On 11 June 1864 the Quartermaster-General telegraphs Canby at Vicksburg that he cannot find the gauge of the Vicksburg and Shreveport Railroad and asks what it is.
items.context: Canby had just taken over the Military Division of West Mississippi after the Red River failure, and rebuilding the Vicksburg–Monroe line was under discussion. Meigs asked again on 17 June ('I have telegraphed you twice', OR I/34 pt 4 pp.424-425), Canby answered on 24 June, and on 27 June Grant endorsed against rebuilding the road (Papers of U. S. Grant vol. 11).
items.what_is_added: Only the code words: Canby, Vicksburg, 'Rail-road' and the Quartermaster-General's signature. The clear words ('I can not find the gauge ... what is it') have been public in the Huntington's volunteer transcription since 2018. The fact that Meigs asked Canby for the gauge is in print through the 17 June sequel. The telegram's own wording was not located in print (N4, D4).
items.why_tier: A quartermaster's technical question whose substance is already in print in the follow-up. Knowing the exact wording and date of the first ask changes nothing in the account.
items.caveats: The G3 check (V1-G3A) marks the N4 'weak': the request is known from the sequel and the clear words are public. NARA RG 92/107 copies are unread.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md D12-V2M and V1-G3A), plus general knowledge of Canby's 1864 command

items.title: Eckert 1864: the Secretary of War to Dana, 6 June 1864, two French officers (N2-T)
items.content: Stanton asks Dana to learn from Grant whether two French officers, a colonel and a captain sent to observe the operations and held back for a week, may go to the front; Grant first declined (7 June), then agreed (18 June).
items.context: In spring 1864 France asked to send officers to observe the war. Seward agreed to receive them in the Union armies only. When the campaign opened, Stanton, on Grant's suggestion, barred visitors from the camps of the engaged army (Foreign Relations 1864). All this came while France was installing Maximilian in Mexico. A Colonel de Chanal appears with Meade's staff in Theodore Lyman's letters of July 1864, so he may be the colonel here. That is plausible, not established.
items.what_is_added: The code words: officers, colonel, captain, operations, Grant, headquarters, front. Most of the sentence frame ('French ... sent to observe the military ... holding them back for a week ... let them go to the ... or keep them away') is public in the Huntington transcription. The topic and Grant's answers are printed in Dana's replies (OR I/36 pt 1 p.91; I/40 pt 1 pp.24-25). The query's own text was not located (N4).
items.why_tier: It adds the observers' ranks and the week's hold-up, which fits the printed visitor ban. The episode itself is known from Dana's printed replies.
items.caveats: The N4 is marked 'weak' by V1-G3A. Three tokens are I-grade (D3, 87%). The officers are not named in the telegram, so the de Chanal identification is my conjecture.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Foreign Relations 1864-65 on history.state.gov (Seward–Dayton on French observers; Bigelow–Seward on Colonel de Chanal's eight-month mission); Lyman's letter of 22 July 1864 on beyondthecrater.com (de Chanal with Meade's staff)

items.title: Eckert 1864: Fry to Manierre (and to W. E. Dodge), 2 Nov 1864, withdraw as a candidate for Congress or resign (E37)
items.content: Provost Marshal General Fry tells Capt. B. F. Manierre, provost marshal of the 8th District of New York, 'Confidential', to withdraw at once as a candidate for Congress or resign as provost marshal, advising the former, and telegraphs the same text to W. E. Dodge, the Union candidate in that district.
items.context: This was six days before the 1864 election. New York's 8th District had a split Union/Republican field (Dodge; Manierre, called 'the republican candidate' in Brooks's contest notice) against the Democrat and administration critic James Brooks. Manierre withdrew the same day: his printed letter (NYT and Tribune, 4 Nov) presents it as his own decision after failed talks with Dodge's committee, and the Tribune called it voluntary. Brooks won the count. Dodge contested the result and was seated in 1866. Brooks's contest notice alleged that Dodge's friends had induced Manierre to retire.
items.what_is_added: The audits located no print of Fry's instruction or of its copy to Dodge, in the Official Records, the press of 1-15 Nov 1864 or the Dodge vs. Brooks record (N3). However, the instruction itself, Fry's name and the copy to Dodge are in clear in the Huntington's public volunteer transcription (pointers 9110-9111). The key adds only Captain, 8th District, New York, Washington, 'telegraphed' and General.
items.why_tier: It documents an order from the Provost Marshal General's office, copied to the Union candidate, behind a withdrawal the press presented as voluntary, in a race later overturned on contest. A historian of the 1864 election in New York, or of Democratic charges of military interference that year, would want to cite it. The significance lies in the document. Our decipherment only fixes the district and state.
items.caveats: The telegram gives no motive. A propriety rule against a serving provost marshal standing for Congress fits the text as well as a partisan one; the copy to Dodge is the politically telling part. N3, not N4: NARA and the Stanton papers are unread. One code word ('Wreath') is unread (D3, 95.7%). The audits' safe sentence does not mention that the clear words are public in the holder's transcription; I read this from the cached sources/mssEC19/p9110-9111.json, and it should be carried into the outward wording.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Wikipedia 'James Brooks (politician)' (Dodge contested and was seated in 1866). The repo's cached Huntington transcription (p9110, p9111) was read directly. Press and contested-election readings are taken from AUD2-LS-C.

items.title: Eckert 1864: F. W. Seward to C. A. Seward, 15 Oct 1864, Havana consuls, Hunter and Tassara; see Evarts (E41)
items.content: Assistant Secretary of State Frederick Seward sends C. A. Seward in New York the names and posts of W. T. Minor and Thomas Savage at Havana, William Hunter of the State Department and Tassara, the Spanish minister, and asks him to see Mr Evarts and ask his cooperation.
items.context: The names match the Arguelles affair. In May 1864, without an extradition treaty, the administration had Marshal Robert Murray seize the Cuban official José Agustín Argüelles, who was accused of selling liberated Africans into slavery, and hand him to Spain at Tassara's request, with Savage at Havana arranging it. It became a campaign issue, and Murray faced a kidnapping prosecution in New York. Clarence A. Seward was the Secretary's nephew and a New York lawyer; William M. Evarts was a leading New York lawyer.
items.what_is_added: Little in words: the names, posts and the request to see Evarts are in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9097). The key adds General, Department, Washington and the street number. No print of the telegram was located (N3).
items.why_tier: If the link holds, it shows the State Department lining up the officials involved and seeking Evarts's help in the Arguelles litigation, a small addition to a known affair. On its face it is only a list of names.
items.caveats: The Arguelles link is inferred (LS-V3: 'plausibly that affair, inferred, not checked'). My searches did not confirm Evarts's role or the date of Murray's indictment. The clear words are public in the holder's transcription, which the audits' safe sentence does not say.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Foreign Relations 1864 (history.state.gov) and Annals of Cleveland on the Arguelles case; a Seward Project entry on Murray (snippet only, page returned 403). The cached transcription p9097 was read.

items.title: Eckert 1864: to John A. Kennedy, New York police, 30 Nov 1864, suspected chief conspirator of the New York fires in the Old Capitol (E46)
items.content: New York police superintendent John A. Kennedy is told that a man believed to be the chief conspirator of the attempt to burn New York, as described in Monday's Evening Post, is in the Old Capitol Prison, and is asked to send someone to identify him.
items.context: On the night of 25 Nov 1864 Confederate agents sent from Canada set fires in a dozen or more hotels and Barnum's Museum. The known conspirators (Martin, Headley, Robert Cobb Kennedy and others) escaped to Canada, and R. C. Kennedy was taken only at Detroit on 29 Dec and hanged in March 1865. A man held in the Old Capitol on 30 Nov as the 'chief conspirator' was therefore apparently a false lead in the first week of the hunt (my inference).
items.what_is_added: Almost nothing in words. The whole substance (chief conspirator, the Old Capitol, 'send on a man to identify him') is in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9130). The key adds 'New York', 'Evening Post' and 'in the'. The Post's description is reprinted in the Evening Star of 29 Nov. No report of the Old Capitol suspect was located in the press of 30 Nov-12 Dec (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: It is a concrete trace of the War Department's early investigation of the plot that a historian of the episode could cite. It does not change the known account, and the suspect is unnamed.
items.caveats: The signature ('M wise well wily Govr') is unread, so the sender is unknown. The 'false lead' reading is inference. The NY Evening Post itself and the Old Capitol records are unread. The clear words are public, which the audits' safe sentence does not say.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Wikipedia 'Confederate Army of Manhattan', Gotham Center and Smithsonian pieces on the 25 Nov 1864 plot (no mention of an Old Capitol suspect found). The cached transcription p9130 was read.

items.title: Eckert 1864: C. A. Dana to Wallace, Baltimore, 7 Nov 1864, a rebel agent calling himself Dr Hamilton (E52)
items.content: Assistant Secretary of War Dana tells Wallace at Baltimore that a rebel agent calling himself Dr Hamilton passed through Elmira going south on Thursday last, six feet two, with light hair, moustache, whiskers and fine teeth, and to catch him.
items.context: It belongs to Dana's arrest orders of 5 Nov for rebel agents in several cities, to be carried out on Monday 7 Nov, the eve of the presidential election. The sibling orders are in clear in the same ledger, and per the audits they are not printed in OR II/7. The Camp Douglas conspirators in Chicago were seized the same night. Lew Wallace commanded the Middle Department at Baltimore.
items.what_is_added: The code words: Rebel, South, the height (6 ft 2 in), the addressee (Wallace) and the signature (Dana). The rest ('agent calling himself Dr Hay mill ton passed through Elmira ... light hair ... fine teeth ... catch him') is in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9117). No print was located (N3).
items.why_tier: A minor addition (a named suspect with his description) to the War Department's pre-election round-up, which itself is visible from the clear sibling telegrams.
items.caveats: The link to the 'Colonel William Hamilton' of E96 is inferred, not shown. The press pass is incomplete (8 of 15 pages unreachable; the Baltimore press is unread). The clear frame is public, which the audits' safe sentence does not say.
items.checked_externally: Web search on Nov 1864 arrests of rebel agents (nothing on this round-up located; Dix's late-October New York measures and the Camp Douglas plot are context). The cached transcription p9117 was read.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Lt Col Biggs, Fort Monroe, 6 Apr 1864, the Spaulding to Hilton Head and the Montauk with two propellers to Annapolis (E62)
items.content: Meigs tells Biggs at Fort Monroe to send the Spaulding on to Hilton Head, to send the Montauk and two other propellers to Annapolis to carry troops to Hilton Head with plenty of coal, and to report his coal on hand and expected, and every steamer arrival daily.
items.context: Shipping for Halleck's order of 5 Apr 1864 sending two colored regiments (1,800 men) from Annapolis to the Department of the South, while troops were being drawn north for the spring campaign. Meigs's 5 Apr order and Biggs's replies of 5 and 6 Apr are printed (OR I/35 pt 2 pp.37-38; I/33 p.814).
items.what_is_added: Almost nothing: the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 8921) gives the message in clear except 'Quartermaster', 'troops' and 'steamers'. The printed exchange around it already carries the ships and orders. No print of this telegram was located (N3, the audits' weakest).
items.why_tier: Routine transport traffic whose substance is in the printed exchange.
items.caveats: One I-grade token. The audits' safe sentence does not say that the body is in clear in the holder's transcription.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md LS-V5, AUD2-LS-F); cached transcription p8921 read

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Ingalls, 27 July 1864, mules shipped and horse shipments stopped (N2-BM)
items.content: Meigs asks Ingalls whether, under changed circumstances, he needs more mules, says about 500 have been shipped and the rest held until he hears, and that shipments of horses to him have been stopped.
items.context: Siege of Petersburg, late July 1864, after the VI and XIX Corps had been diverted to Washington against Early. Ingalls's printed reply of 28 July (OR I/40 pt 3 p.555) says there is no need for more mules until the Nineteenth Corps arrives.
items.what_is_added: The figure 500, 'horses', and the address and signature words. The clear words are public in the Huntington transcription (pointer 9019), and the reply is printed (N3, marked 'weak' by V1-G3B).
items.why_tier: Routine remount and transport logistics. The printed reply already shows the question was asked.
items.caveats: D2 only: no external check of a code value.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md LS-V6, AUD2-LS-G, V1-G3B)

items.title: Eckert 1864: Benham to Humphreys, 16 Mar 1864, the advance bridge train of canvas pontoons ready (N2-BN, Cipher No. 2)
items.content: On 16 Mar 1864 Benham reports to Humphreys that the advance bridge train of canvas pontoons ordered on 29 February will be ready that day, with 50 chess on each chess-wagon though they can be reduced to 42, and the additional wagons sent if still needed.
items.context: The Engineer Brigade at Washington was equipping the Army of the Potomac's bridge trains for the spring (Overland) campaign. Humphreys's order of 29 Feb is printed (OR I/33 pp.616-617).
items.what_is_added: The code words: advance (bridge train), pontoons, the date 29, and the figures 50 and 42. The rest of the sentence is in clear in the Huntington transcription (pointer 8914). No print was located (weak N3).
items.why_tier: An equipment-readiness report answering a printed order.
items.caveats: Weak N3 (two audits): the order it answers is printed. The clear frame is public, which the safe sentence does not say.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md LS-V7, AUD2-LS-H); cached transcription p8914 read

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster General's office to Col. Biggs, Fort Monroe, 20 May 1864 1.30 PM, has Sheridan left the James, must we forage him by the other line (E90)
items.content: At 1.30 PM on 20 May 1864 the Quartermaster General's office asks Colonel Biggs at Fort Monroe whether Sheridan has left the James, and whether they must forage him by the other line.
items.context: After Yellow Tavern, Sheridan's cavalry on its Richmond raid refitted on the James and then moved by White House to rejoin Meade. OR I/36 pt 2 p.852 prints that he left the James on 16 May. Biggs's clear reply of 6.50 PM (Huntington pointer 4642) says Sheridan's command is at White House wanting a pontoon train, rations and forage.
items.what_is_added: Sheridan, left, the James, forage and the address words. The frame is in clear in the public transcription, and the answer is in Biggs's clear reply (weak N3).
items.why_tier: A logistics query whose answer and context are already on record.
items.caveats: Weak N3. The Grant Papers footnotes for these dates were not read page by page.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md LS4-V1a, V1-LS4A)

items.title: Eckert 1864: C. A. Dana to Rosecrans, St. Louis, 7 Nov 1864, no personal description of the Rebel agent at St. Louis (E97)
items.content: On 7 Nov 1864 Dana tells General Rosecrans at St. Louis that the evidence the War Department holds gives no personal description of the Rebel agent at St. Louis.
items.context: This is Dana's answer within the same pre-election round-up of rebel agents ordered for Monday 7 Nov (see E52). Rosecrans's Department of the Missouri had been investigating the Order of American Knights and the Sons of Liberty that year.
items.what_is_added: 'Rebel', 'St. Louis', Rosecrans and Dana. The sentence frame is in clear in the Huntington transcription (pointer 9119). Neither the St. Louis arrest order nor Rosecrans's request was found in OR I/41 pt 4 (weak N3).
items.why_tier: A one-line negative administrative reply. Its only interest is as a trace that St. Louis was in the round-up.
items.caveats: D2 (no external check). The press of the day was unreachable (loc.gov Cloudflare, 8 Oct 2026).
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md FV-LS4-R1b, V1-LS4B); the same web search as E52

items.title: Eckert 1864: Stanton to Maj. Gen. Peck, New York, 3 Sept 1864 8.30 PM, the plot to seize the Sound steamers passed to the Navy (E123)
items.content: Stanton tells General Peck at New York that his telegram about the rebel plot to seize the Long Island Sound steamers has been passed to the Secretary of the Navy, and offers the War Department's help to owners or shippers in guarding or arming their vessels.
items.context: This was one of the maritime plots from Confederate agents in Canada that autumn (the Lake Erie Philo Parsons raid followed on 19 Sept). Peck's report of Collector Barney's detectives (OR I/43 pt 2 p.21) is printed, as is Eckert's forwarding of it to Welles, who sent the Florida to New London (ORN I/3 p.197).
items.what_is_added: Stanton's reply, chiefly the offer to help private owners guard or arm their vessels. The clear frame is in the Huntington transcription (pointer 9062); the key adds telegram, rebel, steamers, Secretary of the Navy and the signature. No print was located (weak N3).
items.why_tier: A small addition to a printed episode: the War Department's response, including the offer to arm private steamers.
items.caveats: Weak N3. The press of the day was unreachable. The Stanton, Peck and Barney papers are unread.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md FV-LS5-B, AUD2-LEDGER-2), plus general knowledge of the 1864 Canada-based plots

items.title: Eckert 1864: General-in-Chief to Hunter, Cedar Creek, 22 May 1864 10.30 PM, not sent: no reinforcements without Grant's orders (E106)
items.content: On the night of 22 May 1864 Halleck's office drafted, and struck out as 'Not sent', a telegram telling Hunter at Cedar Creek that no reinforcements could go to his department without Grant's special orders and that all available troops had been ordered elsewhere by Grant.
items.context: Hunter had replaced Sigel after New Market on 21 May and was about to march on Lynchburg. He had asked for two efficient brigadiers (OR I/37 pt 1 pp.516-517). The replies actually sent on 23 May (E9, 'Energetic and efficient brigadiers are scarce', and a 9 p.m. note on vacancies) are printed (OR I/37 pt 1 p.525).
items.what_is_added: An unsent draft, located in no print. The key adds Hunter, Grant, reinforcements, department, troops, '2 brigades' and Adjutant-General; the frame is in clear in the Huntington transcription (pointer 8969). The draft reads '2 brigades' where Hunter asked for brigadiers, which may be why it was withdrawn; that is my inference.
items.why_tier: It shows a flatter first response, replaced by the conciliatory one that was sent. This is of minor interest for Hunter's campaign and Halleck's handling of Grant's priorities.
items.caveats: Weak N3. A draft never transmitted. Two M tokens (D3, 81%). The brigades/brigadiers reading is uncertain.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md FV-LS5-A, AUD2-LEDGER-1); cached transcription p8969 read

items.title: Eckert 1864 (Fort Monroe ledger): Butler's HQ to Fort Monroe, 2 Nov 1864 2.30 PM, officers, men and guns of five batteries (E160)
items.content: On 2 Nov 1864 Butler's chief of artillery gives Fort Monroe the guns, officers and men of each battery on his list of 1 Nov, for example Battery M, 1st U.S. Artillery, Napoleons, 3 officers and 110 men, and the 17th New York, Napoleons, 4 officers and 166 men.
items.context: Butler was assembling troops to keep order in New York during the 8 Nov presidential election. He asked Grant for 'at least two batteries of Napoleons' (OR I/42 pt 3 p.489). Battery M, 1st U.S. and the 4th New Jersey were the batteries actually sent (OR I/42 pt 3 p.490; Hawley's report, I/43 pt 2 p.559).
items.what_is_added: The strengths and armament of the candidate batteries, not located in the Official Records, Butler's Book or his correspondence (N3). These are numbers, mostly code, so the key adds most of the substance here.
items.why_tier: A minor logistical detail of Butler's election deployment. It gives the strength of one battery that actually went, while the composition of the force is already in print.
items.caveats: The ledger disagrees with itself: E162 lists the 17th New York as 3-inch guns, E160 as Napoleons. The reading was corrected on 8 Oct (FIX-FM1). The 4th New Jersey, which was actually sent, is not on the list.
items.checked_externally: repo only (AUDIT.md FV-FM1, AUD2-LEDGER-3), plus general knowledge of Butler's New York election command

items.title: Eckert 1864: Augur to Meade, 26 Apr 1864, a party needing co-operation from Warrenton and Point of Rocks (N2-R)
items.content: Augur tells Meade (26 Apr 1864, 11.30 AM) that he cannot send the party as he wishes without some co-operation from Warrenton and some from Point of Rocks, and will postpone it if Meade cannot give the force now.
items.context: In late April 1864 Augur's Department of Washington was mounting a small cavalry expedition from Fairfax Court House (Lowell commanding the cavalry, starting 27-28 Apr) into Mosby's country, while Meade's Army of the Potomac was preparing to open the Overland Campaign. Tyler's telegrams to Augur of 26-27 Apr, printed in OR I/33 pp.985-986, already show the 'party from Washington' and when it started.
items.what_is_added: The sentence frame has been public in the Huntington's volunteer transcription of pointer 8948 since 2018 ('I cannot send the party as I wish without some co operation from ... I wish some also from ... of Rocks If you cannot give the ... now I will post pone'). The key adds only Warrenton, 'Point' (of Rocks, which could be guessed), 'Force', the date and time words, and the correspondents (Augur to Meade).
items.why_tier: This is a request for co-operation on a minor anti-partisan expedition whose existence and timing are already printed. Our reading adds two place names and the names of sender and addressee to a sentence that was already legible.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits plus a G3 check; D3, 9/9 H. Not N4 because the Supplement to the OR was not searched. Linking the 'party' to Lowell's expedition rests on Tyler's printed telegrams (the audit's inference). The ledger header day is overwritten, and the date words fix the 26th.
items.checked_externally: Repo only: AUDIT.md sections ECK64-NO2 verifier, D12-V2R and V1-G3A, plus the repo's cached Huntington transcription for p8948, read here. No web check needed.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Biggs, 19 Apr 1864, steamers chartered for Fort Monroe (E21)
items.content: Meigs tells Lt. Col. Biggs at Fort Monroe (19 Apr 1864) that 3 ferry boats and 3 tugs leave Washington at once. Capt. Wise has chartered at Philadelphia and Baltimore 10 side-wheel steamers, 4 propellers, 7 tugs, 2 steam barges and 40 canal barges. Maj. Van Vliet at New York has chartered steamers (George Leary, Helen Getty, Metamora, Champion, Matilda, Highland Light, Richland) and many schooners, and will charter the Warrior and double-decked steam barges for 700 cattle; all are ordered to Fort Monroe.
items.context: This is the quartermaster build-up of the transport fleet that carried Butler's Army of the James up the James to Bermuda Hundred on 4-5 May 1864, timed to Grant's Overland Campaign. Grant wrote to Butler on 18 Apr (OR I/33) that the start could not be fixed earlier than the 27th. Wise's own 19 Apr report from Philadelphia (OR I/33 p.915) prints his vessel list and 'comfortable transportation for 20,000 men'.
items.what_is_added: The vessel names and the plain words were already in the Huntington's public transcription (pointers 8934-8935). The key adds the counts (3 ferry boats and 3 tugs from Washington; Wise's 10/4/7/2/40; capacity for 700 cattle), the places (Washington, Fort Monroe, Philadelphia, Baltimore, New York) and the word 'steam'. Wise's half summarises his own printed report. Van Vliet's New York charters and the cattle barges were not located in print.
items.why_tier: It is a genuine logistics detail for anyone reconstructing the Bermuda Hundred armada, but it changes no known account. The vessel names were already legible, and Wise's part is in OR.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits; D4, 37/37 H. The audit line does not say that the plain words, including all vessel names, are public in the Huntington transcription; I checked this on the cached page. Not N4 because NARA RG 92/107, the QMG letterbooks and HathiTrust are unread.
items.checked_externally: Repo's cached OR I/33 djvu, grepped here for Wise's 19 Apr report (transport for 20,000) and Grant to Butler 18 Apr (not before the 27th). Cached Huntington transcriptions p8934-8935 read. No web search.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Seward to Palfrey, Boston postmaster, 12 Aug 1864, seize Keith's remittance letter to N. Ferris (E38)
items.content: The Secretary of State tells John G. Palfrey, postmaster at Boston (12 Aug 1864, 11 PM), that a letter with a remittance was sent that day from Halifax by way of St Johns by Alex Keith Jr, 'the rebel agent there', to N. Ferris, No. 10 North Market St, Boston. Palfrey is to watch for it, secure it, forward it to him at the State Department and report to the Postmaster General.
items.context: Alexander Keith Jr was the Confederacy's informal agent and forwarder at Halifax. He was involved in the Chesapeake affair of Dec 1863, and in 1875 became notorious as the Bremerhaven 'dynamite fiend'. Bates prints that US authorities had kept a watch on mail addressed to Keith since Dec 1863. E38 belongs to a 12-14 Aug 1864 cluster: E39 to the New York postmaster on three remittances, E40 detaining the schooner Princess, and the Huntington siblings 9816-9820 and 9047, including 'catch Keith who purchased the locomotives'.
items.what_is_added: Most of the order is already legible in the Huntington's public transcription of pointer 9045: Keith, Halifax, St Johns, N. Ferris, Boston, Palfrey, 'very important to the ... to get possession of that letter', and 'forward to me ... State ...'. The key adds 'rebel' (agent), the house number '10 North', 'Government', 'Department', and the signature word read as Secretary of State, which confirms the sender as Seward's office.
items.why_tier: It is a concrete instance of State Department mail interception against Keith's money channel, naming a Boston correspondent, and a historian of Keith or of Confederate operations from Canada could use it. However, the substance was readable without the key, and the standing watch on Keith's mail is already in print. Its weight is mainly as one piece of the E38-E40 cluster.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits; D3, 13/13 H. Flag: unlike N2-R and N2-BM, the status line and safe sentence for E38 do not say that its clear words are public in the holder's transcription. I checked this on the cached page; an outward sentence should carry that clause. N. Ferris is unidentified, and whether the letter was actually seized is not established. Not N4 because NARA RG 59/28, the Seward Papers and HathiTrust are unread.
items.checked_externally: Web search on Alexander Keith Jr (Wikipedia; HistoryNet 'swindling sociopath' article): it confirms his Halifax agency, the Chesapeake role and the 1875 bombing, but found nothing on an Aug 1864 interception. Cached Huntington transcription p9045 read. Repo AUDIT sections LS-V3 and AUD2-LS-C.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Biggs, 25 Apr 1864, winds and waves, 1,000 horses, saddle horses to the Cavalry Bureau (E42)
items.content: Meigs tells Biggs at Fort Monroe (25 Apr 1864) four things. Every exertion is being made, but winds and waves are holding up barges and sailing vessels, and 1,000 horses are being shipped. His requisition for 100 saddle horses went to the Cavalry Bureau. Rucker says Biggs did not send enough transportation for the infantry, artillery batteries and 1,000 horses to go from Washington, so Biggs should send for the mules.
items.context: This comes from the last week of fitting out Butler's James River expedition. Butler had asked on 19 Apr for at least 1,000 cavalry horses, and Halleck promised 1,000 on 21 Apr; both are printed (OR I/33; Butler, Private and Official Correspondence IV p.112).
items.what_is_added: The frame is public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 8945 ('Every exertion is being made ... winds & waves control barges & sail Vessels ... Your requisition for ... saddle ... was referred to ... Bureau ... Rucker info[rmed] ...'). The key adds 1,000 horses, the 100, the Cavalry Bureau, transportation, infantry and batteries. The 1,000-horse shipment it reports is already known from Halleck's printed order.
items.why_tier: This is ordinary quartermaster traffic (weather delays, a requisition routed to the right bureau, a complaint about shipping). Its main fact, the 1,000 horses, is already printed.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits; D3, 28/28 H. 'saddle' is read as plain against the book's value Guard. The audit line does not mention that the plain words are public in the holder's transcription.
items.checked_externally: Repo only: AUDIT sections LS-V3 and AUD2-LS-D, and the cached Huntington transcription p8945, read here.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Lt Col Biggs, Fort Monroe, 6 Apr 1864, the Salvor to Annapolis and coal for Hilton Head (E47)
items.content: Meigs tells Biggs at Fort Monroe (6 Apr 1864, 3.30 PM) to send the steamer Salvor to Annapolis if she is still at Fort Monroe and not under engagements, and to send 1,000 tons of coal afloat at Fort Monroe to Hilton Head if it can be spared, saying how much, so that he can replace it from the North.
items.context: In April 1864 Annapolis was the rendezvous of Burnside's IX Corps, and Hilton Head the base from which Gillmore's X Corps was being shipped north to join Butler. Biggs's offer the same day of a thousand tons of coal, and of coal and water for Salvor, is printed (OR I/33 p.814) and precedes this order.
items.what_is_added: The frame is public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 8922 ('Send Salvor to Ann-a-pole-is if still at ... Order a ... tons of coal afloat at ... to Hilton Heads Advise me how much you can send that I may replace it from the ...'). The key adds 1,000, Monroe (twice), North and the addressee's rank. A second ciphertext copy exists (Huntington 5595).
items.why_tier: These are routine fleet and coal orders. The printed Biggs offer already shows the 1,000 tons, and only the Salvor-to-Annapolis order and the coal's destination are not otherwise located.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits; D3, 92.9%, with one I-grade token (Vintur = Vinton). That the coal was meant to fuel the transports bringing X Corps north is my inference, not stated in the telegram.
items.checked_externally: Repo only: AUDIT sections LS-V4 and AUD2-LS-D, and the cached Huntington transcription p8922. General background knowledge for IX and X Corps movements.

items.title: Eckert 1864: to McCaine at Harper's Ferry for Sheridan, 22 Aug 1864, a train of forges and wagons escorted by the 25th New York Cavalry (E33)
items.content: Washington tells McCaine at Harper's Ferry, for Sheridan (22 Aug 1864), that a small train of forges and other wagons for his cavalry left the day before for Harpers Ferry. It is escorted by the 25th New York Cavalry (350 men, ordered to him) and a detachment of 375 men of the 1st and 3rd Cavalry Divisions, all mounted and equipped.
items.context: These are reinforcements and farriery for Sheridan's cavalry in the opening weeks of the 1864 Shenandoah campaign, when Sheridan had fallen back toward Halltown and Harpers Ferry. The 25th New York Cavalry's assignment to a brigade on 24 Aug is printed in an OR I/43 pt 1 itinerary and in Phisterer.
items.what_is_added: The frame is public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 9055 ('a small train of forges & other wagons for your ... Escorted by the ...'). The key adds the regiment's number, the strengths 350 and 375, Harpers Ferry, 'cavalry', and the 1st and 3rd Divisions.
items.why_tier: This is a movement notice. The regiment's move to Sheridan is already in print, and the added numbers are small detachment strengths.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits; D3, 93.3%. The sender's signature group ('Chisel plane') is unread. A later Huntington telegram (mssEC 18 p.161, 26 Aug) refers to the same forges.
items.checked_externally: Repo only: AUDIT sections LS-V2c and AUD2-LS-F, and the cached Huntington transcription p9055.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Ingalls, City Point, 24 July 1864, cavalry horses and the money shortage checking deliveries (N2-BI)
items.content: Meigs tells Ingalls (24 July 1864) that about 1,000 cavalry horses on hand will be sent at once with the artillery horses, and more as they come in. Depreciation of vouchers and certificates and a short supply of money have lately checked deliveries of horses, and 3,962 cavalry horses have been issued at Washington since 1 July, most of the troopers so mounted to rejoin Grant.
items.context: In July 1864 Early's raid on Washington (11-12 July) had pulled troops and remounts to the capital. At the same time the Union Treasury was short of cash after Chase's resignation on 30 June, so quartermaster vouchers traded at a discount. M. R. Wilson's The Business of Civil War (2006) quotes a contractor that summer complaining of 'the recent severe depreciation of vouchers and certificates'.
items.what_is_added: The voucher sentence was already public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 9011 ('Depreciation of vouchers & certificates & short supply of money have lately checked deliveries of ...'). The key adds what was being delivered (horses), the cavalry and artillery horses, the 1,000, the figure 3,962 cavalry horses issued at Washington from 1 to 24 July, and that the troopers were to rejoin Grant.
items.why_tier: It gives a hard number for remounts issued at Washington in the three weeks after Early's raid, and the Quartermaster-General himself ties the Treasury's money squeeze to slower horse deliveries. Both are useful to historians of the remount problem or of 1864 war finance, though the phenomenon itself is known.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits; D2, 96.7% (29 H + 1 I). The 'rejoin' token is uncertain ('Hotly [?]'). The addressee header reads 'Bickford' on the image; the decoded plain names Ingalls.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT sections LS-V6 and AUD2-LS-G; cached Huntington transcription p9011 read. The finance context is from general knowledge, with the Wilson 2006 quotation taken from the audit. No web search.

items.title: Eckert 1864: to Capt. G. D. Wise, New York, 20 Apr 1864, transports for Butler's expedition (O9-AH)
items.content: Captain G. D. Wise at the Astor House, New York (20 Apr 1864; sender not in clear, probably Meigs), is told to work with Major Van Vliet, who has chartered vessels for the expedition. All vessels should reach Fort Monroe by the 24th and be fully coaled by the 25th, and a colonel reports transport ready for 14,000 men, or 6,000 men and 1,800 horses. Butler wants to move 30,000 men, 2,000 horses, the equipage of ten batteries and 100 wagons, with room for the men to lie down so they are fresh for their morning's work.
items.context: This belongs to the planning of Butler's James River move, which landed at Bermuda Hundred on 5 May 1864. Grant's letter to Butler of 18 Apr (OR I/33) says the start could not be fixed earlier than the 27th, which fits the 24th/25th deadlines here; the campaign actually began on 4 May. Halleck's 16 Apr order sending Wise to Philadelphia and New York, and Wise's 19 Apr report of transport 'for 20,000 men', are printed in OR I/33.
items.what_is_added: Nearly all the figures are in clear in the Huntington's public transcription of pointer 8937: thirty thousand men, two thousand horses, 'of ten', a hundred wagons, 14,000 / 6,000 / 1,800, the 24th and 25th, and 'room to lie down ... fresh for their mornings work'. The key adds the name of the man who 'desires to move' (Butler), the destination (Fort Monroe), and the words Captain, Quartermaster, Major, Colonel, Transportation, Troops, Equipage and Batteries.
items.why_tier: It states Butler's lift requirement and the original late-April timetable, a sharp logistics detail for the Bermuda Hundred landing. But the numbers were already readable in clear, and the rough size of Butler's force (about 30,000+) is well known.
items.caveats: N3 from two audits; D2, 14/14 H, and mostly in clear. The sender is not in clear ('Meigs?'). The key's contribution is attribution and places, not the figures.
items.checked_externally: Repo's cached OR I/33 djvu, grepped here: Grant to Butler 18 Apr ('not earlier than the 27th instant'), Halleck to Wise 16 Apr, Wise 19 Apr ('transportation for 20,000 men'). Cached Huntington transcription p8937 read. Butler's force size is from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster General's office to Lt. Col. H. Biggs, Fort Monroe, 21 Apr 1864, stop everything coming up the Potomac and send it to Fort Monroe (E78)
items.content: The Quartermaster General's office asks Biggs (21 Apr 1864, 3.30 PM) whether his transportation is coming and tells him to report daily by mail. Present orders stop everything coming up the Potomac and send it to Fort Monroe, but a large quantity of transportation ordered for Washington, which will be needed there, should be let through once he is supplied.
items.context: In the days before the spring campaign the transport fleet had competing calls from Washington (IX Corps and the Army of the Potomac's supply) and from Fort Monroe (Butler). Meigs's clear order of 19 Apr diverting Wise's vessels to Fort Monroe is public (Huntington 8934), and Butler's 21 Apr question to Meigs about transport is printed (Butler Corr. IV).
items.what_is_added: The clear words are public in the Huntington transcription (mssEC 18 p.48, pointer 9714). The key adds Potomac, Monroe, Transportation (twice), Report, the question mark and 'as soon as', that is, the places and the object.
items.why_tier: This is administrative shipping coordination whose general shape (vessels diverted to Fort Monroe ahead of Butler's move) is already known from public and printed traffic.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits plus a G3 check; D3, 92.3%.
items.checked_externally: Repo only: AUDIT sections LS3-V18a, AUD2-LS3-A and V1-G3B. Not separately rechecked.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster General's office to Capt. Thomas, Baltimore, 7 Jul 1864 11 AM, return the vessels that brought up Ricketts' troops to City Point with all available steam transports (E92)
items.content: The Quartermaster General's office tells Captain Thomas at Baltimore (7 July 1864, 11 AM) to send the vessels that brought up Ricketts' troops straight back to City Point, together with every steam transport in US service then available in the port of Baltimore.
items.context: Ricketts' division of the VI Corps had been shipped from City Point to Baltimore on 6 July (Grant to Meigs, OR I/40 pt 3) to meet Early's invasion of Maryland, and fought at Monocacy on 9 July. On 9-10 July Grant sent the rest of the VI Corps north by water. That transports were sent back to City Point on the 7th fits, but this is my inference, not established.
items.what_is_added: The order's frame is public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 8996 ('Let the vessels bringing up ricketts ... return at once to ... & send to that place all ... in US service now ... port of ...'). The key adds troops, City Point, steam transports, 'available', 'in the' and Baltimore.
items.why_tier: This is a turnaround order for transports. The movement it belongs to (Ricketts' shipment to Baltimore) is printed, and the order adds only the destination and the scope of the recall.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits; D2, 11/11 H. A sibling QMG telegram to Thomas (Huntington 9777) is still in code. Linking the return to the later VI Corps lift is inference.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT sections LS4-V1a and V1-LS4A; cached Huntington transcription p8996 read. Early's raid and Monocacy context from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster-General to Ingalls, City Point, 9 Aug 1864, steamers engaged and ordered to City Point (N2-CE)
items.content: The Quartermaster General tells Ingalls at City Point (9 Aug 1864, 9.30 AM) that the wagons of the 6th Corps and of the cavalry sent to Washington should follow the troops, because their drivers are needed to relieve Washington's own, and that a large number of steamers has been engaged and ordered to City Point to be ready for any movement in force. If they are not needed there they should return to Fort Monroe and wait events. Ingalls is to consult the commander of the forces on the James, since at City Point the boats would be available to meet any movement in force intended to blockade the river.
items.context: This was early August 1864, after the VI Corps and cavalry had gone north against Early, with Grant besieging Petersburg. Four days later, on 13 Aug, Hancock's II Corps embarked on steamers at City Point for the feint that became Second Deep Bottom. Whether these steamers were that fleet is not established.
items.what_is_added: Much of the frame is public in the Huntington transcription (pointers 9039-9040: '... drivers are needed to relieve ours ... A large number of ... has been engaged and ordered to ... to be ready for any ... return to ... and wait Events ...'). The key adds 6th Corps, cavalry, follow, steamers, City Point, 'movement in force', Monroe, the James, 'available' and 'river'.
items.why_tier: As read, it is quartermaster positioning of wagons and a contingency steamer pool, with nothing that changes a known account. It would become a useful detail only if these steamers were shown to be the fleet used on 13 Aug, which I did not establish.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits; D3, 94.9% (37 H, 2 I). The Deep Bottom link is my own inference from timing, offered as context only.
items.checked_externally: Web search on Second Deep Bottom (Wikipedia, battlefields.org): II Corps embarked on steamers at City Point on 13 Aug 1864. Cached Huntington transcription p9039 read. Repo AUDIT sections FV-LS4-R2b and AUD2-LS4C.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster General to Maj. Van Vliet, New York, 30 June 1864 3 PM, steamers to bring troops from New Orleans (E143)
items.content: The Quartermaster General tells Major Van Vliet at New York (30 June 1864, 3 PM) to dispatch, as they become available, all steamers in service that are fit to bring troops from New Orleans, not to take up ocean steamers not already in service, and to prepare for a large number of troops whose number he has not been told.
items.context: This concerns the transfer of the XIX Corps from Louisiana to Virginia, ordered in late June 1864 (Halleck to Canby 24 June, OR I/34 pt 4; Ingalls 26-27 June, OR I/40 pt 2); part of the corps was diverted to Washington against Early in mid-July. E143 answers Van Vliet's clear 1 PM telegram of the same day listing steamers sailed for New Orleans (Huntington mssEC 10 p.308).
items.what_is_added: The frame is public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 8992 ('all the ... now in service fit to bring ... from ... should be dispatched as they become available ... It is not ... to take up ocean ... not already in service ... I am not advised ... number of ... but am to prepare for a large number'). The key adds steamers, troops, New Orleans, 'necessary' and the QMG signature.
items.why_tier: The programme it serves (ocean transports to bring the XIX Corps north) is printed. Its own instructions, to use steamers already in service rather than charter new ones, are minor administrative detail.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits; D3, 93.3%, with one M token ('whiskey', a spelling variant of the Troops row).
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT sections FV-LS5-B and AUD2-LEDGER-2; cached Huntington transcription p8992 read. XIX Corps context from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Augur to Sheridan, 21 Aug 1864 4 PM, 100 Spencer rifles and 20,000 rounds to Harpers Ferry (E122)
items.content: Augur tells Sheridan (21 Aug 1864, 4 PM) that 100 Spencer rifles with 20,000 rounds of ammunition will be sent to him at once at Harpers Ferry, but that he doubts 100 men are enough for the work they are undertaking.
items.context: This is the reply to Sheridan's printed request of 20 Aug: 'I have 100 men who will take the contract to clean out Mosby's gang. I want 100 Spencer rifles for them' (OR I/43 pt 1 p.860, approved by the War Department on 21 Aug). That request is the origin of Capt. Richard Blazer's Independent Scouts, armed with Spencers, whom Mosby's men routed at Kabletown on 18 Nov 1864.
items.what_is_added: Much of the reply is public in the Huntington transcription of pointer 9053, including 'Spencer rifles', 'rounds of ... for them will be sent you at once to ...', 'I doubt if a ... men are sufficient for the work they are undertaking' and the signature Augur. The key adds the addressee (Sheridan), the numbers 100 and 20,000, 'ammunition' and Harpers Ferry. This ties Augur's doubt explicitly to the 100-man anti-Mosby party.
items.why_tier: It gives the Washington department commander's quotable scepticism about the Blazer plan, plus the ammunition issue. It is minor because the request, its approval and the Spencers' issue to Blazer's men are already printed, and the doubt sentence was legible without the key.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits; D3, 81.8%. Treating Augur's doubt as 'borne out' at Kabletown is hindsight; the telegram makes no prediction beyond the doubt.
items.checked_externally: Web search on Sheridan's 100 Spencer rifles and Blazer's Scouts (Wikipedia 'Blazer's Scouts', NPS 'Mosby's Rangers in the Shenandoah Valley'), which confirms the request and Kabletown. Cached Huntington transcription p9053 read. Repo AUDIT sections FV-LS5-A and AUD2-LEDGER-1.

items.title: Eckert 1864 (Fort Monroe ledger): Turner to Butler at Fort Monroe, 9 Dec 1864, steamers loaded to follow the Fort Fisher expedition (E163)
items.content: Brig. Gen. J. W. Turner tells Butler at Fort Monroe (9 Dec 1864, 11 AM) that he thinks one or two large steamers should be loaded with subsistence, forage and ammunition, ready to follow at a moment's notice.
items.context: Butler's first expedition against Fort Fisher was assembling at Hampton Roads; it sailed on 13-14 Dec and its landing failed on 25 Dec. Turner was Butler's chief of staff (OR I/42 pt 3). By common accounts the army transports later had to put into Beaufort, N.C., for coal and water while waiting for the navy, which gives the advice some interest as background.
items.what_is_added: The body is largely in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (mssEC 25, pointer 5823). The key adds 'steamer', the number 2, Butler, Monroe and Turner's rank.
items.why_tier: This is a staff officer's logistics suggestion whose words were mostly legible already. The expedition and Turner's role are well documented.
items.caveats: Weak N3 from two audits; D2, 10/10 H. No external check of the content. The Beaufort coaling episode comes from my general knowledge and is not in the repo's audit.
items.checked_externally: Repo only: AUDIT sections FV-FM1 and AUD2-LEDGER-3. Fort Fisher context from general knowledge; no web search.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Howell to Ingalls, 8 Mar 1864, water transportation at Yorktown and cavalry horses (N2-AI)
items.content: Captain Wm. T. Howell, assistant quartermaster, tells Brig. Gen. Ingalls on 8 Mar 1864 at 3.30 PM four things. Rucker has sent all his available water transportation to Yorktown, and Biggs at Fort Monroe has been ordered to send what he has. A large steamer has been ordered from New York. There will be transport at Yorktown for 1,000 men and horses by the next evening. The first lot of the 1,400 cavalry horses being bought arrives tomorrow, and Captain Feilner has been notified.
items.context: The Kilpatrick-Dahlgren raid on Richmond (28 Feb-3 Mar 1864) ended with Kilpatrick's survivors in Butler's lines on the Peninsula. They were shipped from Yorktown back to Alexandria, and that shipment is already printed (OR I/33 pp.650, 662). Ingalls was chief quartermaster of the Army of the Potomac, Rucker the depot quartermaster at Washington, and Biggs Butler's chief quartermaster at Fort Monroe.
items.what_is_added: The clear words of the ledger entry are in the Huntington's public volunteer transcription. The period Cipher No. 2 book gives the 40 code words that carry the specifics: Yorktown, Fort Monroe, New York, 1,000 men and horses, 1,400 cavalry horses, tomorrow, Kilpatrick, and the ranks. No printed text of the telegram was located (verifier class N3, two audits). The event it served is in print.
items.why_tier: This is quartermaster traffic arranging the return of a raid force whose shipment from Yorktown is already documented. The figures (transport for 1,000, 1,400 remounts) are ordinary logistics. They do not touch the raid's controversy or change its account.
items.caveats: Depth D4 (40/40 H), a solid reading. N3 rather than N4 because RG 92/107/393, the OR Supplement and OR ser. III vol. 4 are unread. The text does not tie the 1,400 horses to Kilpatrick's division. 'Cap Feilner' as Capt. John Feilner, 1st U.S. Cavalry, is the auditor's conjecture.
items.checked_externally: Repo only for the reading and the print search (AUDIT.md D12-VP and D4-V2AI). I compared the volunteer transcription on disk (ciphers/eckert-1864/sources/mssEC19/p8910.json). The raid context is from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: G. V. Fox to Olcott, 2 May 1864, investigate the New York Navy Yard only, not prosecute (E23)
items.content: Assistant Secretary of the Navy Fox telegraphs Col. H. S. Olcott on 2 May 1864 at 9 PM. Olcott is not to proceed against anyone in the New York Navy Yard: he is commissioned to investigate only, not to prosecute, and the Secretary of the Navy will prosecute on the facts Olcott collects. Solicitor Whiting gave his opinion on certain points only that day. Olcott is to report each case ready for examination when his evidence is complete.
items.context: Henry Steel Olcott had investigated War Department fraud since 1862. In February 1864 he became the Navy Department's special commissioner for contract fraud in the navy yards; Fox's commissioning letter of 18 Feb 1864 is quoted in Olcott's own 1879 essay. He is better known as co-founder of the Theosophical Society (1875). William Whiting was the War Department's solicitor. The telegram shows the Navy Department keeping prosecution decisions with Welles early in Olcott's inquiry.
items.what_is_added: Almost all of the message is in clear in the ledger, and so in the Huntington's public volunteer transcription (pointer 8955). The key adds only seven code words: Colonel, New York twice (it is the New York yard), Secretary of the Navy twice (he prosecutes) and Report. No printed text was located in Olcott's 1879 account, Fox's 1865 Senate letter, OR/ORN or the press (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: It is a real glimpse of the limits placed on a controversial fraud investigator, and Olcott's biographers and historians of Navy procurement fraud could use it. But the substance was already readable in the public transcription, and the decode adds mainly the yard's location and who held the authority to prosecute.
items.caveats: Only 7 code tokens. Depth D3, with no external check of a decoded value. The letter from Olcott that Fox answers ('Letter recd') is not identified.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT.md (LS-V1, AUD2-LS-A; the Olcott and Fox printed accounts were read there). I read the volunteer transcription on disk (p8955.json). Olcott's later career and Whiting's office are from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Seward to Wakeman, New York postmaster, 12 Aug 1864, three Keith remittances to be seized (E39)
items.content: Seward, signed by code word as Secretary of State, telegraphs Abraham Wakeman, the New York postmaster, on 12 Aug 1864 at 11.30 PM. Alexander Keith Jr. at Halifax sent three remittances that day by way of St John: to N. Ferris, 10 North Market St, Boston; to J. B. Hunter & Co, New York; and to Gordon Bruce & Co, New York, with directions to ship at once to Mitchell Kenner & Co, Montreal. The letters are to be secured at all hazards and sent to Seward with information on the addressees' trade or business. The telegram is Wakeman's authority, and he is to report to the Postmaster General.
items.context: Alexander Keith Jr. was the Confederate agent at Halifax. He was involved in the Chesapeake affair (Dec 1863) and later became notorious as the 'Dynamite Fiend' of the 1875 Bremerhaven explosion. Wakeman had already intercepted Keith's cipher mail in Dec 1863; those are the letters the War Department telegraph office decrypted, as Bates recounts. Sibling Huntington telegrams of 10-14 Aug ('Spare no means to catch Keith who purchased the locomotives'; Gordon Bruce & Co supplying machinery for Keith) show a coordinated State, War and Post Office effort against his purchasing network.
items.what_is_added: The firm names, the addresses and the order to seize are in clear in the ledger and in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9045). The key adds the sender's identity (Byron = Secretary of State), New York, the street number, 'information', 'report to the Postmaster General' and the date. No printed text was located (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: It shows State Department mail interception reaching named Northern and Canadian firms in Keith's supply chain, a concrete detail for historians of Confederate agents in British North America. But the names were already readable in public, and the key adds chiefly the attribution to Seward.
items.caveats: Depth D3. The sibling telegrams (pointers 9816-9820, 9042, 9047) are transcriptions, not decoded here. What the seized letters contained, if any were seized, is not known from the repository.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT.md (LS-V3, AUD2-LS-C: Bates, Foreign Relations 1865, Larabee's The Dynamite Fiend, NYT and Chronicling America). I read the volunteer transcription on disk (p9045.json). Keith's later identity is from general knowledge and the audit's Larabee citation.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Rucker to Biggs, 29 May 1864, coal for White House; City of Albany and Ranger back (E43)
