items.content: Rucker telegraphs Lt. Col. Biggs at Fort Monroe on 29 May 1864 at 5.30 PM. He asks whether the coal for the York and Pamunkey rivers, telegraphed for on the 27th, has been sent, because it is needed at White House at once. He reports that the steamers City of Albany and Ranger left that day for Fort Monroe with General Benham's command and its horses. He asks that both boats be sent back at once to move cattle and horses up the Pamunkey.
items.context: In the last days of May 1864, as Grant crossed the Pamunkey toward Cold Harbor, the Army of the Potomac moved its supply base from Port Royal to White House Landing. Benham commanded the Engineer Brigade (the pontoon trains). Biggs's reply of 30 May, promising the two boats back, is printed in OR I/36 pt 3.
items.what_is_added: Most of the body is clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 8975). The key adds horses, Fort Monroe, Benham's command, 'telegraphed on the 27th', 'left today' and 'river'. The printed reply shows only the boats' return; Rucker's coal question and his reason for wanting the boats are not in print (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: Ordinary depot-quartermaster traffic for a change of base that is already well documented. It adds no fact of consequence.
items.caveats: D3, 95.2%. One word is unread ('Waymorners') and one is flagged ('River's[?]').
items.checked_externally: Repo only (AUDIT.md LS-V3, AUD2-LS-D). I compared the volunteer transcription on disk (p8975.json). The White House base context is from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Col Biggs, Fort Monroe, 11 Aug 1864, the Continental to Hilton Head with the General-in-Chief's dispatch (E50)
items.content: Meigs telegraphs Col. Biggs, quartermaster at Fort Monroe, on 11 Aug 1864 at 11.30 AM. Biggs is to provision and water the steamer Continental 'to bring whiskey from the Department of the South'. As soon as a dispatch the General-in-Chief is preparing is ready, he is to send her with it to Hilton Head and report her hour of sailing. A tail note says the General-in-Chief's dispatch has gone forward.
items.context: On 10 Aug Ingalls had sent the Continental to Fort Monroe and asked that her orders go through Biggs (OR I/42 pt 2, printed). On 11 Aug Halleck wrote to Foster, commanding the Department of the South at Hilton Head: 'Lieutenant-General Grant directs that you will send to Washington all the troops you can possibly spare, remaining yourself purely on the defensive' (OR I/35 pt 2 p.231). This was part of Grant's stripping of coastal garrisons after Early's July raid, as Sheridan took over in the Valley; Foster reports on the same page that Birney's brigade of 3,500 had left the day before. That order is very probably the dispatch the Continental carried.
items.what_is_added: Part of the body is clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9042). The key adds 'from the Department of the South', General-in-Chief, 'as soon as', quartermaster and 'report'. What history gains is the vessel and the timing of the sea passage that carried the order; the order itself is in print. No printed text of this telegram was located (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: These are shipping arrangements for an order whose text is printed. It is ordinary quartermaster traffic.
items.caveats: Two words are unread ('amirs', and 'ham', probably 'hour'). The plain-looking 'whiskey' is very probably the key's Whisky = Troops (key.md p.24 l.7), misspelt as the audits ruled for E100 and E143. Read that way, the order is to bring troops from the Department of the South, not 'bring her from' it as the depth sentence says; the repository has not regraded it. Linking the dispatch to Halleck's 11 Aug letter to Foster is my inference: neither audit's log cites OR I/35 pt 2 p.231 for E50 (LS-V4 searched that volume only for the Continental's own wording). Under the E49/N2-BL lesson on forwarded orders, a verifier should weigh whether it affects E50's class.
items.checked_externally: I read OR ser. I vol. 35 pt 2 pp.231-232 in the repository's cached IA djvu text (sources/ia-fulltext/print-check/warofrebellion352unit_djvu.txt.gz): Halleck to Foster, 11 Aug 1864, and Foster to Hatch, 11 Aug 1864 (Birney's brigade gone). Also the key.md row Whisky = Troops and the volunteer transcription p9042.json.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Capt. Thomas, quartermaster, 8 Apr 1864, the steamer Relief to Annapolis for colored troops (E57)
items.content: Meigs tells Captain Thomas, quartermaster, on 8 Apr 1864 at 4 PM: if on examination the Relief is a good, staunch steamer, she is to call at Annapolis for a load of colored troops; if not needed there, she is to go on to Hilton Head and report for duty.
items.context: Halleck's memorandum of 5 Apr 1864 ordered two colored regiments (1,800 men) at Annapolis to South Carolina. The 5-6 Apr telegrams between Meigs and Biggs about the Spaulding and Montauk carrying them are printed (OR I/35 pt 2 pp.37-38; I/33 p.814). This is one of the vessel orders carrying out that plan.
items.what_is_added: Most of it is clear in the public transcription (pointer 8927); the key reads 'collared whisky' as colored troops and adds steamer, quartermaster, captain and the sender's office. The plan is printed; this vessel order was not located (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: One of several ship orders executing a plan that is already printed. Ordinary logistics.
items.caveats: D3, 80% (two I tokens). Thomas's station is uncertain in the header ('at Annapolis?').
items.checked_externally: Repo only (AUDIT.md LS-V5, AUD2-LS-F). I compared the volunteer transcription on disk (p8927.json).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Secretary of War to Dana, 4 June 1864, Lt Col Wade, the Senator's son, for Sheridan's staff (N2-BJ)
items.content: The Secretary of War asks C. A. Dana on 4 June 1864 at 10 PM to find out whether Sheridan will take on his staff Lieutenant Colonel Wade, the Senator's son. Wade served as a captain of cavalry in the Army of the Potomac and distinguished himself for pluck and gallantry; he has just returned from New Orleans and wants to serve under Sheridan. Meade knows him.
items.context: Dana was Stanton's confidential observer at Grant's headquarters during the Overland Campaign, and the telegram went the day after the main Cold Harbor assault. The officer is James F. Wade, son of Senator Benjamin F. Wade, chairman of the Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War and co-sponsor of the Wade-Davis bill passed that July. Heitman lists the son as lieutenant colonel of the 6th U.S. Colored Cavalry from 1 May 1864 and colonel from 19 Sept 1864, brevetted for Beverly Ford in 1863.
items.what_is_added: Almost all the meaning is in code: Dana, Lieutenant Colonel, Captain, Cavalry, Army of the Potomac, New Orleans, Sheridan, Staff, Meade, Report, Secretary of War. The public transcription shows only 'Wade Son ... Senator ... pluck & gallantry'. No printed text was located in Dana's Recollections, Sheridan's Memoirs, the Grant Papers vols 10-12 or the OR (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: A small, specific patronage episode: Stanton personally using Dana, in the week of Cold Harbor, to place a powerful Radical senator's son on Sheridan's staff. It is of interest to biographers of Stanton or Wade but changes no military account, and the telegram does not show the outcome.
items.caveats: Depth D2 (one I token). Whether Sheridan took him is not established in the repository; Heitman's register suggests he stayed with his colored cavalry regiment. The tail 'cable still remains broken' is an operator's note.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT.md (LS-V6, AUD2-LS-G, including Heitman, Dana and Sheridan's memoirs). I read the volunteer transcription on disk (p8979.json). Senator Wade's role is from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864-65: the Quartermaster General's office to Van Vliet, New York, 3 Jan 1865, steamers for 1,000 construction-corps men to Savannah and 4,000 troops from Baltimore (E66)
items.content: On 3 Jan 1865 the Quartermaster General's office tells Brig. Gen. Van Vliet at New York that its request of the night before, for a report of steamers available there, is unanswered. Colonel Wise has called for steamers to take 1,000 men of the U.S. Military Railroads construction corps from Baltimore to Savannah. Steamers are also needed to take 4,000 troops from Baltimore to sea, destination not reported, with coal and water for 15 days. Van Vliet is to report the vessels he can send and dispatch them unless countermanded.
items.context: After Sherman took Savannah (21 Dec 1864), the War Department sent Military Railroads construction men there (McCallum to Sherman, 29 Dec, OR I/44 p.834). It also sent about 4,000 troops from Baltimore to garrison the city, Grover's division (Sherman to Grant, 16 Jan 1865, OR I/47 pt 2 pp.59-60). Van Vliet's two replies of 3 Jan on the few steamers available at New York are printed (OR I/46 pt 2 p.28).
items.what_is_added: The key carries the operative content: Van Vliet, Baltimore, Savannah, 1,000, 4,000, steamers. But both movements and Van Vliet's replies are in print, so the decode adds only the Quartermaster General's own request in its wording, including 'destination not reported' (weak N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: A shipping request for two movements already documented as events, with the replies printed.
items.caveats: D3, 86.8% (4 I and 1 M token, 'Waymomers'). Weak N3: a clear copy in the Huntington's Sent volume would lower it. 'Pandora Wise' is Colonel George D. Wise, as corrected by LS-V7.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (AUDIT.md LS-V7, AUD2-LS-H).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Halleck to Canby, New York, 22 Apr 1864, is the 14th New York Artillery drilled as infantry so that it can go into the field? (O9-BA)
items.content: On 22 Apr 1864 Halleck asks Canby at New York what condition the 14th New York (Heavy) Artillery is in: has it been drilled as infantry so that it can go into the field, or only to man guards, bridges and the like?
items.context: In spring 1864 Grant pulled heavy-artillery regiments out of the Washington and coastal garrisons to fight as infantry. The print already gives this regiment's strength and departure (Canby to Stanton, 21 Apr, OR I/33 p.938) and its outcome, 'armed as infantry, has been assigned to your corps' (Halleck to Burnside, 23 Apr, p.955). It fought with the IX Corps from the Wilderness on.
items.what_is_added: The body is clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9717) except the code words Artillery, Infantry, Guards, Bridge and Halleck's signature. Those come from the War Department's older vocabulary (mssEC 67). Halleck's question itself was not located in print (weak N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: A one-line status query sitting between two printed telegrams that already give the regiment's arm and fate.
items.caveats: Depth D2, 71.4% (5 H of 7; 'Randolphed' and 'wedlock' M). Weak N3: AUD2-LS3-B notes a third audit could draw N2 from p.955.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (AUDIT.md LS3-V18a, AUD2-LS3-B).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Capt. Geo. K. Leet to Lt. Col. Bowers, 14 Aug 1864, Sharpe's men and W. J. Lee's offered ride to Gordonsville (N2-BZ part 2)
items.content: On 14 Aug 1864 Captain Leet in Washington tells Lt. Col. Bowers at Grant's headquarters that Colonel Sharpe's men will not go out before Wednesday or Thursday, saying they cannot get information by starting sooner. A man named W. J. Lee, formerly employed by Sharpe, offers to ride to Gordonsville starting tomorrow morning if given a horse and 200 dollars. Sharpe's men vouch for him as a good and reliable man.
items.context: In mid-August 1864 Grant's headquarters was trying to learn what Lee had sent toward the Shenandoah: Anderson, with Kershaw's division and Fitz Lee's cavalry. On 10 Aug Bowers asked Leet to have the men sent by Col. George H. Sharpe, head of the Bureau of Military Information, find which way troops from Richmond had passed from Gordonsville, and how many. That request is printed in a note of the Grant Papers vol. 11. The same leaf carries Lincoln's printed telegram to Grant on house burning (part 1).
items.what_is_added: About half the body is clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9047), including W. J. Lee's name and offer. The key gives Gordonsville, horse, Wednesday/Thursday, information, tomorrow and the 200 dollars. Leet's answer to the printed request was not located in print (weak N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: A small, concrete piece of Union intelligence practice: Sharpe's network slow to move, and a freelance scout naming his price for a ride to Gordonsville. Historians of the Bureau of Military Information could use it, but it records an offer, not a result, and changes no account.
items.caveats: Depth D2 (one M token, 'Black'). The Grant Papers vol. 11 notes for 14 Aug were not read page by page, so the weak N3 could still fall. Whether W. J. Lee went is not known from the repository.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT.md (LS4-V1a, V1-LS4A). I read the volunteer transcription on disk (p9047.json). Context on Sharpe and Anderson's detachment is from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: T. T. Eckert to City Point, 18 Dec 1864 11.15 PM, tell Rawlins that Grant left Washington by boat at 3 PM (N2-CK)
items.content: At 11.15 PM on 18 Dec 1864, T. T. Eckert in Washington has the City Point operator tell General Rawlins that Grant left Washington by boat for City Point at 3 PM that day.
items.context: In mid-December Grant had come to Washington meaning to go on to Nashville and take over from Thomas. Thomas's victory at Nashville (15-16 Dec) made the trip unnecessary, and Grant returned to City Point. The Washington Evening Star of 19 Dec reported his departure by dispatch boat the afternoon before, giving 1 o'clock. Meade asked Rawlins on 19 Dec when Grant would arrive (OR I/42 pt 3 p.1038).
items.what_is_added: The key gives General, Grant, left, 3 PM, today and City Point; the frame and 'Raw lines' are clear in the public transcription. The fact itself was public the next day. What remains ours is this telegram and its departure hour, which differs from the press's 1 o'clock (weak N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: A movement notice whose substance was in the Washington press the following day.
items.caveats: The time word gives 11.30 PM against the header's 11.15 PM. The 3 PM against the Evening Star's 1 o'clock is unresolved. The Grant Papers vol. 13 note pages are unread.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT.md (FV-LS4-R2b, AUD2-LS4C, including the Evening Star of 19 Dec 1864 p.2). Grant's aborted Nashville trip is from general knowledge (his Personal Memoirs).

items.title: Eckert 1864: Capt. Geo. K. Leet to Lt. Col. Bowers, City Point, copy to Sheridan, 12 Aug 1864, Hill's brigade to Early, Fitz Lee at Orange C.H., Longstreet in the Valley (E145)
items.content: On 12 Aug 1864 Captain Leet in Washington reports to Lt. Col. Bowers at City Point, with a copy to Sheridan at Winchester, what scouts just arrived say. A brigade of Hill's corps was sent to Early the previous Friday while its division was under marching orders. Fitz Hugh Lee's cavalry was at Orange Court House on Wednesday night, the 10th. Longstreet is in the Shenandoah Valley, his corps supposedly with him. The scouts know nothing of the force mentioned in Bowers's dispatch of the 10th. The Central railroad is not running beyond Beaver Dam.
items.context: In early August Lee sent R. H. Anderson, with Kershaw's division of Longstreet's corps and Fitzhugh Lee's cavalry, toward Culpeper and Front Royal to support Early against Sheridan, newly in command in the Valley. Longstreet himself was still recovering from his Wilderness wound and did not return until October, but Union reports put 'Longstreet' in the Valley. Sheridan wrote to Grant on 13 Aug that reports 'confirm your telegram that Longstreet is in the Valley, and that Fitz Lee's cavalry ... was at Orange Court-House' (OR I/43 pt 1 p.784). Modern campaign studies quote that line. Sheridan fell back toward Halltown over the following days.
items.what_is_added: About half the body is clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9044). The key supplies the military substance: corps, brigade, division, Hill, Fitz Lee, cavalry, Orange C.H., Longstreet, Shenandoah, force, City Point, Winchester. Two clauses reach print only as Sheridan's acknowledgement, which does not name Leet, and Bowers's 10 Aug dispatch that E145 answers is printed in the Grant Papers vol. 11. Not located in print: the Hill's-brigade, marching-orders and Beaver Dam clauses, and Leet as a source of the Longstreet report (weak N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: The fullest item in this set: a plausible Washington-scout source for the 'Longstreet is in the Valley' misreport that Sheridan acknowledged, plus three further intelligence items. But its key clauses are already in print as Sheridan received them, Leet's telegram of 11 Aug (E120) fits Sheridan's reply equally well, and the report is largely wrong. It sharpens provenance rather than changing the account.
items.caveats: Depth D2 (90.6%; three M tokens: 'France', 'Beaver' and 'Brussells' = Shenandoah). 'Hill's' rests on the key's History = Hill. In the reading, 'wolves' (= scouts by key.md, as in E104) and 'melds' are left unread, and '[New York] [Orange C.H.]' is taken as 'at Orange C.H.'. That Sheridan's 'your telegram' is E145 rather than E120 is unproven.
items.checked_externally: Repo AUDIT.md (FV-LS5-B, AUD2-LEDGER-2). On 8 Oct 2026 I ran an Internet Archive full-text search (be-api) for 'Longstreet is in the Valley': Sheridan's 13 Aug line is quoted in the Grant Papers vol. 11, Lowry's Fate of the Country (1992) and McLean's California Sabers, so historians know the misreport. Two earlier be-api calls returned 502; one retry answered. Google Books was unavailable (daily quota, HTTP 429), so I did not check secondary works such as Feis's Grant's Secret Service. Anderson's detachment and Longstreet's absence are from general knowledge.

items.title: Eckert 1864: Meade (Washington) to Humphreys, 4 Mar 1864, send scouts to Fredericksburg (E104)
items.content: On 4 Mar 1864 Meade, in Washington, acknowledges Humphreys's dispatch about the scouts and tells him to send scouts down to Fredericksburg and below to find out whether the enemy has any force on this side of the Rappahannock or on the Northern Neck.
items.context: This is Meade's reply to Humphreys's printed report of 4 Mar 1864, 10 AM, on scouts returning from the country of the Kilpatrick-Dahlgren raid (OR I/33 p.639). Humphreys, chief of staff, was in charge at headquarters while Meade was in Washington. The printed sequel of 7 Mar (p.651, a Richmond paper on Kilpatrick returning by the Northern Neck) shows why the Northern Neck mattered.
items.what_is_added: The frame is clear in the public transcription (pointer 8907). The key gives scouts (twice), Fredericksburg, enemy, force, Rappahannock and Meade's signature. The reply was not located in print (weak N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: A routine reconnaissance order answering a printed report, in seven code groups.
items.caveats: Weak N3 with only seven code groups. The Meade papers and the press are unread for this item; the Grant Papers were covered only by snippet search.
items.checked_externally: Repo only (AUDIT.md FV-LS5-A, AUD2-LEDGER-1). I compared the volunteer transcription on disk (p8907.json). The raid context is from general knowledge.

items.title: Jan and Lodewijk van Nassau to William of Orange, Dillenburg, 22 Oct 1573 (WVO 5797): two of the subjects Groen van Prinsterer printed as undeciphered read under Lodewijk's 1574 table with the names from the contemporary 5550 gloss
items.content: Two of the blanks Groen left in his print of the letter (Groen IV, Lettre CDXLIV) each yield one name. On p.5 the reading is 'Bey dem Herzog von Sachsen und [Landgraf] ... ist willens ...': with the Duke of Saxony and the Landgrave, someone is willing to press Orange's cause and to hinder the election of a King of the Romans. On p.7 it is '[Pfaltzgraf] ... helt sich wol und thut in warheit viel': the Palatine holds firm and in truth does a great deal. The other codes in both blanks are unread (136 and 146 on p.5, 146 on p.7), so the subject of 'ist willens' is still unknown.
items.context: In October 1573 Orange's brothers at Dillenburg were lobbying the German Protestant princes and the Wetterau counts' union for help in the Revolt. They were also trying to block Maximilian II's plan to have one of his sons elected King of the Romans (Rudolf was elected in 1575). Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate was the Nassaus' strongest German backer. Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel and Elector August of Saxony held back: Schmidt 1989, p.286, as checked in AUDIT.md, has Wilhelm refusing the plan.
items.what_is_added: Groen printed the whole letter in 1837 (N0 for the letter). What is ours is two name values placed into two of his blanks. The codes were located with our own letter table, and their values come from a period interlinear gloss on the sibling letter WVO 5550. No prior decipherment of the blanks was located (N4).
items.why_tier: Filling an editorial blank in a standard edition is a genuine addition, but a minor one. The second audit (A2.2) states that the Palatine value adds no fact that was not already known: the Palatine's support is in Kluckhohn 1872 and Blok 1889. The Landgrave value shows that Saxony and Hesse were the princes to be worked on, which matches what is known. The one element that could matter, who was willing to lobby them and to obstruct the election, sits in the codes that are still unread.
items.caveats: Depth is D2 at 11.1% (6 of 54 non-null tokens). Each blank is read only in part: 3 of the 4 codes on p.5 are unread or nulls, and 146 is unread on p.7. The two values rest on one clean gloss each. The second 5550 attestation of 153 is partly obscured (V8.2). The fr18 judge FAILs on the spots file, which is below the judge's length. A clear copy at Wiesbaden (HHStAW 170 III) or Marburg is unsearched and could lower the class.
items.checked_externally: Repo: AUDIT.md sections V8, A2, SO-LODEWIJK-5797, DEPTH-REGRADE and G3, reading_5797_full.txt, and the Groen IV CDXLIV text on disk (groen/groen_IV_CDXLIV.txt), read around both blanks. Wider context from general knowledge of the 1573 Nassau and German-princes diplomacy. No new web search for this item.

items.title: August of Saxony, cipher enclosure of 1561-64 (WVO 53, Nassau papers): read cryptanalytically, no key or sibling decipherment
items.content: Orange's cipher postscript to Elector August (Breda, 24 Oct 1561) passes on news from Spain: the Prince of Spain is to marry his father's sister and then come to govern these lands. It adds that the Duke of Vendome means to recover his kingdom of Navarre 'mit der gute oder krieg' (by agreement or by war). Orange gives his own view that, the King of France being so young, the Navarre plan will come to nothing.
items.context: Orange had married Anna of Saxony, Elector August's niece and ward, at Leipzig in August 1561, and reached Breda on 4 October. This is one of his first letters to his new in-law, and it already uses cipher. The news is court rumour of the season: Don Carlos marrying his aunt Juana and coming to the Netherlands, and Antoine de Bourbon (King of Navarre, Duke of Vendome) pressing Philip II over Spanish Navarre while Charles IX was eleven. A contemporary Dresden newsletter (WVO 56) carries the Prince-to-the-Netherlands and Navarre items, but not the marriage or Orange's opinion.
items.what_is_added: Both audits found no prior decipherment and no printed plaintext of this postscript (N4); a twentieth-century KHA Collectie Japikse copy is unseen. The rumours themselves are in print from other senders. What is ours is that Orange sent these particular rumours to Saxony in cipher in October 1561, together with his own one-line judgement on Navarre. The key is ours, recovered by cryptanalysis.
items.why_tier: The content is news and rumour that circulated widely in 1561, and the only element in Orange's own voice is a brief opinion. It is useful to a historian of the early Orange-Saxony relationship, as a sign that Orange was acting as an intelligence channel to August from the start. It changes no known account of Habsburg marriage policy or of the Navarre question.
items.caveats: This is a cryptanalytic reading with no H or C tokens: S 356, M 8 of 364 (D3 at 97.8%), described as a proposed reading. It is backed by a matched control at 99.3% but has no external check. The Collectie Japikse copies, which a WVO editor names as the likeliest place for an earlier decipherment, have not been seen. I could not confirm the specific 1561 Carlos-Juana rumour on the web; AUDIT.md says it is common in print.
items.checked_externally: Repo: AUDIT.md sections A2.4, D2, Huysman reply, R11A-AVSV/AVSV2 and both G3 checks, plus reading_53.txt. One web search on the 1561 Don Carlos and Juana rumour (no specific hit; general Carlos background only). Wider context from general knowledge.

items.title: Elector August to Orange, Torgau 18 Nov 1561, cipher enclosure (WVO 57, KHA A 11/XIV B/41-6)
items.content: August tells Orange in confidence that a few days earlier the Emperor had asked him, through a formal embassy, to help elect his son Maximilian King of the Romans in the Emperor's own lifetime. August expects the other Electors to be asked the same, and asks Orange to keep it secret.
items.context: In autumn 1561 Ferdinand I began sounding out the Electors on electing Maximilian in his own lifetime. The result was the Frankfurt election of November 1562, which ended Philip II's earlier hopes of the imperial succession. Orange was Philip's councillor and stadholder, and had just married August's niece. The clear text of the same letter, summarised in Demandt's regest no. 113, carries harmless news about Sweden, England and a feud. The cipher held the political secret.
items.what_is_added: The imperial approach is in print (Goetz 1891; Kluckhohn I no. 148 gives the Palatine side, December 1561). What our reading adds is the channel: that August told Orange about it in cipher within days and asked for secrecy. It also dates the embassy to Saxony to shortly before 18 November 1561. No prior decipherment was located (N4). The key is a period one, rebuilt from the contemporary decipherment of sibling WVO 74.
items.why_tier: Of these items it is the clearest and best supported, and it shows the Hidden part of a letter whose clear part has a published regest. It also shows August confiding imperial-succession business to a servant of Philip II, which is of interest to historians of Orange's German connections. The event itself, however, is already in print. That sharpens a known relationship but does not change the account of the 1562 election, so it falls short of notable.
items.caveats: Depth is D3: C 294 of 301 (97.7%), with 7 M tokens, mostly word-signs. August's minute in Dresden (Loc. 9941/3 f.268-269, with a 'Zettel') has not been seen and may carry the enclosure in clear, which would lower the class to N0 in substance. Whether Goetz already dates the Saxon embassy as exactly was not checked by me.
items.checked_externally: Repo: AUDIT.md sections A2.4 (with the Demandt regest), D2, V8 DNOK re-check, Huysman reply and G3, plus reading_57.txt. One web search on the November 1561 imperial embassy to Saxony: no specific source found, only general 1562-election background.

items.title: Lodewijk van Nassau to William of Orange, four cipher letters 1573-1574 (WVO 4610, 4611, 4612, 4616): partial reading with a key aligned from two sibling letters' decipherments
items.content:
The cipher stretches of 4610, 4611 and 4616 read only as fragments.
- 4610 (3 Jun 1573) mentions the Electors, a proposed convocation of the Electors' councillors, three hundred horse ready to risk the journey to Holland, French captains' offers, Strasbourg, the Duke of Alencon, Fregoso and 'Gaspar', and the Palatine and the Landgrave.
- 4611 (2 Jul 1573) reports a rumour that Alba is raising forces to join those that have come to him, and asks for news of Haarlem, about which various rumours are running. It also names a captain Rudolff and the Count van den Berghe in connection with companies for Friesland.
- 4616 (12 Apr 1574, camp at Weeze) is about finding quarters near Goch for the next day, possibly on the Duke of Cleves' land, and ends 'nous verrons demain lequel sera le meilleur'.
- 4612 does not read.
items.context: In 1573 Lodewijk was the Revolt's main diplomat in Germany, working with French agents (Fregoso, Gaspard de Schomberg) and the Protestant princes for money and troops, while Haarlem was under siege; it fell on 12-13 July 1573. In spring 1574 he led the army down the Maas and was killed with his brother Hendrik at Mookerheyde on 14 April 1574, two days after 4616. Orange's printed replies (Groen IV, CDXXVII, CDXXXIII, CDLXXXIV) acknowledge 4610, 4611 and 4616 but do not repeat their cipher content.
items.what_is_added: Groen printed none of the four letters. What is ours is the partial reading of their cipher stretches with a period key, aligned from the contemporary decipherments of WVO 4613 and 4615. No prior decipherment was located for 4610, 4611 or 4616 (N4); 4612 is N3 and has no reading. The substance visible in the fragments matches the known outline of the 1573 French-German-Nassau negotiations, the Haarlem crisis and the 1574 march.
items.why_tier: The letters themselves are high-level correspondence, but the reading is fragmentary. No letter reads straight through, so no passage can be quoted as a clean statement. What can be taken from the fragments is logistics and confirmation: the three hundred horse, a convocation of councillors, quarters near Goch two days before Mook, and the Haarlem rumours. That is genuine but minor detail on events already documented in outline.
items.caveats: Depth is D2 at about 63% (C 2512 of 4012 at audit; four letters 58.3% C/H on the newer basis). Most C tokens come from clear words and keyed word-signs; the homophonic letter runs read as unbroken strings. The verifier's D2 sentence for 4610 ('il fault que on pardonne ... ce lundy ... la rechute') is almost all clear text in the token file, not cipher. Several fragments, including captain Rudolff's offer, rest on M or I grades. Name codes of 145 and above differ by direction of correspondence; 'hollande' in 4616 is M. 4612 is unread, possibly a different table.
items.checked_externally: Repo: AUDIT.md sections V2, D1, V8.3, R12-LVNV and G3, NOTES.md, and the full readings and token files for 4610, 4611 and 4616. One web search on Fregoso, Schomberg and Louis of Nassau in 1572-73: it confirms both men as French agents dealing with Louis and the German princes, documented in Groen III-IV. The Haarlem and Mookerheyde dates are from general knowledge.

items.title: SHStA Dresden Loc. 694/08 f.410, Manteuffel to Flemming, Berlin, Nov 1712: unglossed cipher P.S. read with Dr. Krauske's 1893 manuscript key table (Loc. 694/10, unprinted)
items.content: Fragments of Manteuffel's November 1712 postscript to Flemming read under Krauske's table: the Swedes, 'la paix', 'ne donne contentement', and Stettin. The Queen of England is named three times, once 'touchant le prince' and once followed, after two unread groups, by 'ne fera rien pour lui, mais luy ...'. Who 'the prince' and 'lui' are is not read.
items.context: In the Great Northern War, autumn 1712, Stenbock's Swedish army was in Pomerania facing Danish, Saxon and Russian forces. Prussia was neutral but had its eye on Stettin, and Britain under Oxford and Bolingbroke was pressing for peace in the North while avoiding commitments. Manteuffel was the Saxon envoy in Berlin, reporting to Flemming, the leading minister of Augustus II.
items.what_is_added: Krauske's key table of 1893 is unprinted, and the passage is not among the extracts of these reports printed in Acta Borussica, Behördenorganisation I (1894), nor quoted in Droysen IV.1 or IV.2. What is ours is the application of that table to this unglossed postscript, giving fragments (N4, key `published` in rule 10's sense). The general news themes are well documented.
items.why_tier: This is diplomatic reporting, not administrative traffic. Even so, the readable fragments contain nothing a historian could cite: the Swedes, peace, Stettin and the Queen of England's attitude are the ordinary news of that season. The one potentially specific statement, about the Queen and 'the prince', lacks its referents. Its value so far is methodological (the key opens these reports), not historical.
items.caveats: Depth is D2 on one recurring code only (217, Queen of England, in two independent contexts). The cipher clause fails: the longest letter run is 11 against an authentication distance of 380. Grades are C 144, M 49, U 23 of 216, and the fr18 judge FAILs. The table may have been built from the period glosses, so it carries their values but is not tested independently on unglossed codes. The press of November-December 1712 is only partly searched.
items.checked_externally: Repo: AUDIT.md sections VERIFY-MANT, AUDIT2-MANT, GAPS180, R9-MANTV, DEPTH-MH and G3 (V1-G3D), plus reading.txt and NOTES.md. Northern War and British-policy context from general knowledge and from the sibling 0391 audit (V-MANT08). No new web search.

items.title: Linhares dictionary code: the book is Vieyra's 1809 pocket dictionary, and the letter fragment reads
items.content: The 26 number groups on the leaf decode against Part I of Vieyra's 1809 London Portuguese-English pocket dictionary into broken Portuguese ('para supprir o seu lugar junto com man o d justa he segredo ate para o ministerio / pela memoria do cagar lhe pauperr ven ha logo'); the only clause that reads clearly says that something 'is a secret even from the ministry'.
items.context: The item comes from maço 86 of the Condes de Linhares papers at ANTT. The repository's own sibling sweep found that this maço is mainly the family papers of João Paulo Bezerra de Seixas. The item carries no date, sender or recipient. The key sheet's worked example ('a guerra de França com a Rússia parece inevitável') points to 1811-12, when Rodrigo de Sousa Coutinho, 1st Count of Linhares, was secretary for foreign affairs and war at Rio (he died in January 1812) and Bezerra was Portugal's envoy at St Petersburg. The other face of the leaf, read on 2 Oct 2026, is a clear French billet to or about 'Madame la Comtesse' and 'B.a', ending 'Brûlez ceci. Seu Desgostadissimo'. That 'B.a' could mean Bezerra is my guess only; the repository does not say so.
items.what_is_added: The main addition is identifying the codebook behind a period Portuguese dictionary code: Vieyra's 1809 pocket dictionary, Part I, in which all twelve worked-example groups land on the exact word. This key is 'ours' (rule 10). The second addition is a reading of the 26 groups (H 23, M 3). The verifier found no prior print of the letter, no prior decipherment of this key and no prior naming of its dictionary (N3 for both items, two audits plus a G3 check).
items.why_tier: Showing that a commercial London bilingual dictionary served as the book for a Portuguese family or diplomatic book code of about 1811-12 is a genuine, citable small addition to the history of Portuguese cryptography. The message itself names no one and carries no date. About a quarter of its tokens are trimmed word-fragments, so it gives nothing a historian could attach to an event beyond 'secret even from the ministry'.
items.caveats: Novelty is N3, not N4: the sender-family edition, Textos Políticos (1993), has never been opened (LOCAL-QUEUE L10). Depth is D2. The 88.5% figure is a token grade: line 3 does not read as prose and three tokens are M (cagar, justa, para). AUDIT.md and the depth sentence still treat m0002 as pages 2-3 of a longer letter with pages 1 and 4 lost, and call it a 'surviving page'. NOTES.md (NEXT-LIN, 2 Oct 2026) later found it to be a single complete half-sheet billet whose verso is the French note, so the 'fragment' wording in the audit is stale. Part II of the dictionary (English) is untested. Whether the key belonged to Rodrigo's Rio secretariat or to Bezerra's circle is inference.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Adams Papers slip file (masshist.org) shows João Paulo Bezerra signing the Russo-Portuguese treaty at St Petersburg on 29 May/10 June 1812, and Wikipedia's list of foreign secretaries shows him later succeeding Araújo (Barca) at Rio in 1817. Everything else comes from the repository (AUDIT.md sections 1-11, NOTES.md 'm0001 fetched and read', 'Who it likely served', LX-SIB).

items.title: Gramont to Villandry, Rome, 20 May 1530 (BnF fr. 2980 f.29r)
items.content: In the cipher of his letter to the king's secretary Villandry, Gramont says he has handed the bearer an article he set apart and addressed on the outside to Villandry, although it is for the King. He asks Villandry to demand it of the bearer 'car c'est le total fondement'. He says he showed someone everything 'pour le contenter et oster ... de suspecon', which is why he made the article separate, and asks that something be handled secretly ('secretement').
items.context: Gabriel de Gramont, bishop of Tarbes (created cardinal on 8 June 1530), was Francis I's envoy in Rome from April to June 1530. The Peace of Cambrai had just been made, Florence was under imperial and papal siege, and France was pressing Clement VII on Henry VIII's divorce. The same day Gramont sent the King an all-cipher letter (f.30, no.22) about 'la liberté de Florence' and the city's force 'entre vos mains'. The audit names f.30 as the likely 'article apart' but marks this as inference. Imperial agents were taking French despatches at the time: Mai reports a Gramont courier stopped at Florence, and Loaysa reports letters intercepted at Asti. That explains the care over routing.
items.what_is_added: A partial reading, with Tomokiyo and Lasry's published Gramont 1530 key, of the cipher in a letter whose existence and date were already catalogued (BnF 1868; Catalogue des actes de François Ier IX) but whose content had never been printed. Tomokiyo had flagged the letter as readable and Bourdeau catalogued it; neither gave a reading. The verifier's class is N4, 'no prior decipherment located'.
items.why_tier: The cipher shows how Gramont protected the core of his business: a separately routed 'article' carrying 'le total fondement', sent under cover of the secretary and kept away from suspicion. That is a real but small point about diplomatic practice and channels. The covering note does not say what the business was; any substance would be in f.30, which is a different item and now graded D1.
items.caveats: The reading is partial and rests on one reconciled sign transcription corrected by a blind second reader (568 signs: H 532, S 1, M 30, U 5). About two lines read as continuous French; the rest is undivided or doubtful. Several words are conjectures: 'fondement' is read 'tondement' in the decode, and the opening is better divided 'j'ay baillé'. That f.30 is the 'article' is inference. The key is published, not ours.
items.checked_externally: The historical context comes from the repository's own audit citations (Catalogue des actes IX, CSP Spanish IV.1 pp.560-61, Heine/Loaysa 1848, Archivio storico italiano App. I for the April letter) plus general knowledge of the 1530 Rome and Florence situation. No new external lookup was made for this item.

items.title: Danzay to the Cardinal of Lorraine, dated 27 Jan 1557 (BnF fr. 20140 f.35-36)
items.content: In fragments, Danzay's cipher mentions the King of Denmark and a promise 'qu'ils s'en ploieroient volontiers'. It mentions the chancellor, who 'peult beaucoup', and 'the passions and affections of those' whose help he needs. On f.36r it describes sending by way of Augsburg and 'les marchans de Lion' 'avecques le peu de perte pour le change'.
items.context: Charles de Danzay was the French resident in Denmark from 1548 to 1589. Here he writes to Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, who with the Guises dominated Henri II's policy. The date may be 27 January 1558 new style, because the French year then began at Easter. Either way this is the 1557-59 war with Philip II after the truce of Vaucelles failed, when France wanted Christian III's goodwill in the north. The crown's credit ran through the Lyon merchant-bankers and German houses such as those of Augsburg, so the money passages fit that system. Teulet (1851) wrote that Danzay's correspondence before 1567 'n'a pu être retrouvée'.
items.what_is_added: A reading of the cipher runs of an early Danzay letter, using the key Tomokiyo published in 2026 (H 546 of 705 across f.35 and f.36r). The leaf has no contemporary decipherment. Ryabov 2025 (Quaestio Rossica) reconstructs a different Danzay table from letters of 1574 and 1578 and does not touch this one. Verifier class N4, two audits.
items.why_tier: The fragments confirm Danish royal and chancellery involvement and a money channel through Augsburg and Lyon merchants in Danzay's business of 1557/58. That is a minor documentary point from a poorly documented phase of his mission. They do not state the purpose, the sums or the parties to any agreement, so they cannot change an account of Franco-Danish relations.
items.caveats: Partial: about 23 of 37 lines are continuous French, 70 signs on f.35 are unkeyed, and the f.35v/f.36r join plus three stretches on f.36r are unread. The reading rests on one reconciled transcription. About 150 clear-hand words, never enciphered, carry much of the sense. The year may be old style. The money-transfer sense of 'pour le change' is partly the solver's grade-I inference. The key is Tomokiyo's.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Wikipedia and the Daussy summary give Danzay's Copenhagen residence as 1548-89, and nothing turned up specific to 1557. The date-style point, Teulet's 'correspondance n'a pu être retrouvée' and Ryabov 2025 come from the repository's AUDIT.md (first audit section 4, V6, V1-G3D).

items.title: William Stamford to Thurloe's office, Calais, 13 March 1655 (Birch 1742 vol. 3 pp.188-189): keyed reading of a letter printed without its decipherment
items.content: In the cipher runs Stamford says the matter came to his knowledge 'by meere chance' and 'without the least iniunction of secrecy', from a person who took it for granted that he was involved when he met him 'stealing out of England'. He says it is 'a plot hath been a hatching' by 'the whole partie of [code 143]', and that betraying it would make him 'irreconcilable with them as long as I live'. He calls it 'a more general rising' with more people engaged 'than in any of the former ones'.
items.context: 13 March 1655 new style is 3 March old style. That is five days before the date set for the royalist general rising (8 March O.S.) and nine days before Penruddock's men entered Salisbury (12 March). Stamford was a royalist exile at Calais offering to betray the plot to Cromwell's government ('your friend', the Protector) in return for protection and reward. Macray's Rawlinson index names Col. Kelsey as his correspondent. Thurloe's office already knew much about the conspiracy from other sources.
items.what_is_added: Only the wording of the cipher runs. Birch printed the clear text in 1742, along with the office's endorsement summarising the letter as an offer of 'discovering of the plott'. Birch also printed the office's decipherment of Stamford's 30 March letter, which restates 'the substance of my former letters'. The key is 'period', rebuilt from those printed sibling decipherments, and agrees with Tomokiyo's published Stamford table on every value in this letter. Verifier class N4.
items.why_tier: The substance, an informer's offer to betray the March 1655 rising, is already in print in the clear text, the endorsement and the deciphered 30 March letter. The cipher adds only how he came to know of it and his phrasing about 'the whole party' and a 'general rising'. The one name code (143) is unread.
items.caveats: In the input list this item's slug was 'AUDIT.md'; its folder is ciphers/thurloe-printed, item P4. About a third of the cipher (144 numerals in printed p.188 lines 53-61, mixed with clear tokens Birch set, such as 'am', 'it', 'in') gives letters but no sentences. The depth re-check says the outward figure is about 66% of the cipher reading as text, although the token grade is 97.9%. The Bodleian leaf (MS Rawl. A. 24) has not been seen, so a contemporary decipherment on it is not excluded. The addressee is uncertain (Thurloe or Kelsey).
items.checked_externally: Web search on the Penruddock rising: Wikipedia, the BCW Project and the Wagstaffe biography give 8 March 1655 as the planned date and 12 March for the entry into Salisbury, both old style. The rest comes from the repository (AUDIT.md P4 sections, THUR-P4-DEPTH, the Birch 30 March decipherment on disk).

items.title: Blathwayt papers addenda, Madrid and Port Ste Marie intelligence 1727-1729 (Huntington mssBLA 184, 186, 191(a)): reading with a key rebuilt from seven deciphered items of the same run
items.content: The cipher reads only in part. In BLA 186 (Madrid, 13 Sept 1728, a letter about Ripperda's escape) it gives 'l'ambassadeur [?] a été fort [?] [ce]tte affaire' and 'Monsieur de Patiño m'en a parlé ce soir'. In BLA 191(a) (Port Ste Marie, 1729) the writer thanks 'milord' and complains that Mr Keene 'm'aime' but has no orders concerning him. He says he helped in 'the past affair' without ever being told what he could offer toward the accommodation, and asks to be sent orders. BLA 184's name codes are unread.
items.context: Rose's Marchmont Papers (1831) identify the writer of BLA 186 as the Abbé G.B. Pareti, a Modenese resident in Spain who fed intelligence to the Earl of Marchmont and the British government for a stipend; 191(a) is probably his too. Ripperda, the fallen Spanish minister, escaped from Segovia on 2 Sept 1728. In 1729 Benjamin Keene was negotiating the Anglo-Spanish accommodation that became the Treaty of Seville (Nov 1729). Marchmont forwarded 191(a) to Newcastle from Cessnock on 8 Aug 1729.
items.what_is_added: Readings of cipher lines with a key of 395 groups rebuilt from the contemporary decipherments of sister items in the same run (grade C, key 'period'). Rose printed the clear part of BLA 186 in English in 1831, showing the cipher only as '(Cypher.)'. The cipher lines and 191(a) were not located in print (N4 for the cipher; N1 for BLA 186's clear text).
items.why_tier: This is ordinary traffic from an intelligence agent. One part is a paid informant's grievance about his standing and lack of orders during the Seville negotiations. The other is a two-line note that Patiño discussed the Ripperda affair with him, in a letter whose clear text is already printed. It shows the agent had access to Patiño but changes nothing about the episode.
items.caveats: Partial: C 131, M 20, U 21 of 172 tokens after the A4-RFHUN revision. Four groups in the BLA 186 p1 line are unkeyed, so the ambassador's reaction is unread. 'milord', 'serai' and 'ignorance' rest on M or unkeyed groups. Pareti's authorship of 191(a) is inference. The copy sent to Newcastle has not been traced and could carry a period decipherment. BLA 184 yields only three syllables.
items.checked_externally: Repository only: the Rose 1831 match and the London Gazette check are in AUDIT.md (second audit, V2-G3GAPS). The Ripperda, Keene and Seville context is general knowledge.

items.title: BnF fr.3251 no.86, Lodovico Birago to the Duke of Nevers, Saluzzo, 27 August 1572: the whole cipher read with Tomokiyo's published 1572 key
items.content: In fragments, Birago writes that the men of Carmagnola 'remain troubled'. He names the Huguenots (a code word) three times, including two captains who 'are both Huguenots', and says the 'baron de Sadres' (des Adrets) made himself odious over past matters. He mentions close dealings ('pratica stretta') over the government with 'the baron' and, he believes, with Sanfrè, and fears that by wanting to do the service he may earn 'la mala gratia d'altri'.
items.context: Lodovico (Ludovic) Birago, kinsman of Chancellor René de Birague, held command in the French marquisate of Saluzzo and wrote to Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, who was responsible for France's Piedmont holdings. Carmagnola was a French fortress that Savoy wanted back. The letter is dated three days after the St Bartholomew massacre in Paris (24 Aug 1572), almost certainly before the news could reach Saluzzo. So its Huguenot worries are pre-massacre garrison concerns. Birago died on 28 Dec 1572.
items.what_is_added: A cryptanalytic reading (grade S, no H or C) of all the letter's cipher, using Tomokiyo's published 1572 Nevers-Birago key, which beats 200 shuffled keys at five seeds. The leaf has no period decipherment. None was located in either volume of the 1665 Mémoires de Nevers or elsewhere (N4, two audits).
items.why_tier: It records Huguenot officers in the Carmagnola garrison and a commander's unease about his standing on the eve of the massacre, a real local detail for French Piedmont in August 1572. It is fragmentary and states no plan, order or number.
items.caveats: Of 758 tokens: S 629, M 76, U 53, H 0, C 0. The language judge FAILs and most lines do not read through. The identifications of des Adrets, Sanfrè and Geneva come from the grade-I gloss. The letter's long clear prose (ff.170r-177r) may carry more of the substance than the cipher. I could not tie des Adrets' 'odious' conduct to a known event.
items.checked_externally: Web searches on Birago's office in 1572 were inconclusive, and the English Wikipedia article on des Adrets has him on the royal side from 1567, with no 1571-72 episode. The context comes from the repository: AUDIT.md cites Catherine de Médicis' Lettres IV naming Ludovic de Birague in command at Saluces after 24 Aug 1572, and his death on 28 Dec 1572.

items.title: BnF fr.3251 no.90, Lodovico Birago to the Duke of Nevers, Saluzzo, 2 October 1572: cipher of ff.184r-185r read with Tomokiyo's published 1572 key
items.content: In fragments, Birago writes of a negotiation with a count, articles he sent, and 'captain Scipione Carego'. He says that 'after the execution' the house of Montmorency 'remains in some suspicion' and many are 'stunned and doubtful'. He mentions a stronghold ('serraglio') 'in favour of the Huguenots', and a Francesco Ga..o who presented letters and asked for money and a subsidy. He writes that someone 'has his mind on the government' of Turin, that over religion there will always be 'confusions and difficulties' to the prejudice of the service, and uses phrases about making 'the Queen' understand and about what 'depends on the house of Montmorency'.
items.context: Five weeks after St Bartholomew (24 Aug 1572), the court presented the killings as an 'execution' that forestalled a Huguenot plot. The Montmorency clan were widely suspected of sympathy with the Huguenots: Marshal François, absent from Paris, and Damville in Languedoc. Birago held the French places in Piedmont under Nevers and died three months later.
items.what_is_added: A cryptanalytic (S-grade) reading with Tomokiyo's published 1572 key of all the letter's cipher. Every portion has had two audits and no prior decipherment was located (N4).
items.why_tier: A French commander in Piedmont noting in cipher that the Montmorency house stayed under suspicion after 'the execution', alongside worries about a Huguenot-held stronghold, would interest a historian of the massacre's aftermath in the provinces. But the reading is fragmentary and fails the language judge. The key identifications ('the execution' as the massacre, 'the Queen' as the Queen Mother, Montmorency's role) are the glossator's inferences. As read, it echoes a well-known theme rather than sharpening it. It could rise to notable if a firmer transcription confirmed the Montmorency passages.
items.caveats: Of 966 tokens: S 730, M 124, U 111, H 0, C 0. The judge FAILs. The 20-sign f.185v run is not licensed by its own control. The gloss is grade I throughout. 'Memoransi' rests on a sign the key does not cover, read in context as M. The clear prose of the letter has not been brought into the significance assessment.
items.checked_externally: No item-specific external check. A web search on Birago's 1572 office was inconclusive. The Montmorency and St Bartholomew context is general knowledge. The repository's own searches (AUDIT.md VERIFY-NEVBIR-90REST, AUDIT2-NEVBIR-90R) found 'casa di Momoransi' only in Davila and narrative sources, not this letter.

items.title: Baluze 170 f.229r-v: Chavigny to d'Avaux, Amiens, 25 Aug 1640, bare cipher passage on the junction of the dukes' and the Landgravine's troops with Longueville
items.content: Chavigny tells d'Avaux that 'le S. Salvius' should send credentials to [code 73, Tomokiyo 'Bavier', probably Banér] to satisfy the dukes and the Landgravine on the conditions they want for joining their forces with either crown's army or both. They want their troops joined to Longueville and under his command even when the two crowns' armies are together. If the Landgravine is put off by [73's] excessive firmness, 'nous perdrons les seuls adherents' and each will withdraw shamefully, 'laissant l'ennemi maistre de la campagne'. And 'on gratiffiera le comte d'Heberstein qui luy doit succeder' to bind him to do better than his predecessor.
items.context: The court was at Amiens just after the fall of Arras (9 Aug 1640). D'Avaux was at Hamburg, where he dealt with the Swedish resident Salvius. In 1640 the Swedish army under Banér, the French-Weimarian army under Longueville and Guébriant, and the Hessian and Brunswick-Lüneburg contingents campaigned together in central Germany amid quarrels over command. Peter Melander (Holzappel) resigned the Hessian command in mid-July 1640 and later went over to the Emperor. Kaspar von Eberstein was the Hessian lieutenant-general who took over.
items.what_is_added: A reading, with Tomokiyo's published D'Avaux key, of a cipher passage that has no period decipherment on the leaf. DECODE lists the letter as 'Decrypted' but holds only the key. No print of the passage was found in Avenel, Le Clerc, the Guébriant histories, Acta Pacis Westphalicae I 1, Boppe 1887 or Grotius' Briefwisseling (N3, two audits).
items.why_tier: The passage states two French intentions: a gratification to secure the loyalty of the new Hessian commander a few weeks after Melander's defection, and the line France took in the allied command dispute (German allied troops under Longueville rather than the Swedish marshal, for fear of losing 'the only adherents'). That is the kind of hidden instruction a historian of Franco-Hessian relations in 1640 would cite, provided the reading holds. The tier is provisional on the caveats.
items.caveats: Novelty is N3, not N4. The AAE Correspondance politique and Hessian or Lüneburg-side editions such as Rommel VIII are unchecked, and either might record the Eberstein gratification. Depth is D2 with only 29% of tokens at H: the 106 numerals are H, and all 180 letter signs, including the whole Eberstein clause, are M. AUD2 notes the letter signs were transcribed 'settled from context', so they are not independent of the reading. Code 73's value is contested: the key's 'Bavier' (Bavaria) against a contextual Banér. That the predecessor is Melander is inference.
items.checked_externally: Web search: Deutsche Biographie and Wikipedia via search say Melander resigned the Hessian command in mid-July 1640 and changed sides; Deutsche Biographie lists Kaspar von Eberstein as a Hessian lieutenant-general. A search did not explicitly confirm that he succeeded Melander, though Noailles 1913, cited in the audit, places Eberstein at the head of the Hessian troops in 1640. Context also draws on AUDIT.md (Grotius 4813/4836 on Longueville stalled on the Rhine).

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: two telegrams, Fox to Butler and Meigs to Butler, 21-22 Apr 1864
verdicts.reason: This is the best-attested reading in the group: N4 and D4, two ledger copies, and a blind second reader agreeing on 96% (AUDIT.md 'N4 set', 'Depth'). Historically, though, it adds almost nothing. E4's decision is already in print: Fox's telegram to Ericsson about the camels, sent ten minutes earlier (ORN I/9 p.667), and Butler's reply ('your camels', 'sink the obstructions', OR I/33 p.279). E5's horses are in print (Halleck, OR I/33 p.938), and so is the move of the Tenth Corps fragments to Fort Monroe (OR I/33 p.940). V1-G3A's diff found only three things not in print: the 4,000-men figure, 'you have all the transportation', and 'at the cavalry depot'. These are small logistical details. The reader's own why_tier says it 'changes nothing'. The context is accurate: Plymouth surrendered on 20 Apr 1864 after the Albemarle sank the Southfield, Butler held the Department of Virginia and North Carolina, and the Bermuda Hundred landing was on 5 May. Checked: AUDIT.md sections 5-6, 'N4 set', 'Depth' and V1-G3A, and reading.md E4/E5. No new external search.
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: replace 'The two figures not in print are 4,000 men instead of 3 regiments and the horses waiting at the cavalry depot, along with you have all the transportation' with: 'Not located in print: "4,000 men here for [Fort] Monroe instead of 3 regiments", "You have all the transportation and should send it up for them", and that the 1,000 horses (themselves in print, Halleck to Butler, OR I/33 p.938) were waiting at the cavalry depot.' Also note that the 8-foot bar is itself in print (Fox to Ericsson, ORN I/9 p.667), so '8 feet' is ours only as a code word. Outward class wording: 'no prior decipherment located (verifier class N4)', always together with the AUDIT's clause that most of the words have been public in clear in the Huntington transcriptions since 2018.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Judge Advocate Turner, 10 Oct 1864, Jewett and Siebert from Richmond; Gemmell in the Old Capitol (E27)
verdicts.reason: In the public transcription (cached sources/mssEC19/p9091.json) the frame is in clear: the four names, 'came from ___ last week', 'supposed to be ___ agents', 'Gemmell ___ the ___ with them & is now in Old Capitol', and Miss Gardner going to Norwich after 'teaching ___'. The key fills in Richmond, Rebel, New York, crossed, Potomac, Connecticut and South. A reader of the frame could already guess most of these. None of the four people is identified, and the outcome is unknown. This is an ordinary counter-intelligence tip, one of many that autumn. The context about Turner is accurate. Horan, Confederate Agent (1954) p.226 likewise describes 'Major Turner' and his agents investigating informants in the same weeks (Internet Archive dli.ernet.157117, read this session). The reading is D3 (93%), with 'Grunt' M and the addressee 'beverage' unread.
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: replace 'Two audits found no print, press report or prison record naming any of the four' with 'Two audits found none of the four named in print, in the 1864 press (Chronicling America) or in the Old Capitol prison memoirs; the prison's own records and NARA M797 (the Turner-Baker case files) were not read.' Keep 'harem' unexplained in the content line; 'Harlem' is a guess and should stay in the caveats only.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Seward to Murray and Harrington to Barney, 13 Aug 1864, detain the schooner Princess (E40)
verdicts.reason: Almost everything that makes this item interesting was already readable in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (cached p9046.json). That includes 'Detain the Princess and her cargo for further orders', 'Detain Schooner Princess and with aid of U S Marshal examine her cargo', the addressees Robt Murray and Hiram Barney, 'Geo Harrington Acting' and the Boston tail note. The key adds New York, the 3 PM time word and the titles in the signatures. Even the Seward signature carries a [?], and 'nick' is unread. The tie to Keith is inferred from neighbouring telegrams, not stated, and the outcome is unknown. Taken alone, this is a one-line detention order. The context facts are accurate: the Keith siblings 9816-9820 and 9047 are as AUD2-LS-C records, and Keith was behind the Bremerhaven explosion of December 1875.
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: replace 'The joint State/Treasury order to stop and search a named schooner' with 'Little in words: both detention orders, the addressees (Murray, Barney), Harrington's name and the tail note are in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9046); the key adds New York, the 3 PM time and the officers' titles in the signatures (Secretary of State, [Acting Secretary of the] Treasury). No press report of the detention was located (two audits).' In context, add after the sibling list: 'whether the Princess carried anything of Keith's is not stated in any of these telegrams.'

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Rucker to Newport, Baltimore, 29 Nov 1864, every available steamer and propeller (E45)
verdicts.reason: I checked the context against the repo's cached OR I/43 pt 2 (warofrebellion432unit) and it is partly wrong. Sheridan had already confirmed the move on 28 Nov at 8 p.m. ('I send the Sixth Corps to you by divisions ... commencing on the 30th') and at 9.30 p.m. (OR I/43 pt 2 p.683). Halleck's 1 p.m. telegram of 29 Nov (p.695) was not pressing Sheridan. He was asking whether the Gordon report should stop the detachment, because 'the President and Secretary of War both think it useless to send it away at present'. 'Please answer immediately, as I have ordered steamers here' was the reason he needed a quick answer. So the fact that steamers were ordered to Washington that morning is already in print. E45 adds only that Rucker called up Baltimore's boats at about 10.45-11 AM. That is routine logistics, and the link to the Sixth Corps is still inference.
verdicts.wording_fix: context: replace 'On 28 Nov 1864 Grant asked Sheridan for the Sixth Corps, and Sheridan said he would start it by divisions on the 30th. At 1 p.m. on 29 Nov Halleck pressed Sheridan, ...' with 'On 28 Nov 1864 Grant asked Sheridan for the Sixth Corps, and Sheridan replied at 8 and 9.30 p.m. that it would start by divisions on the 30th (OR I/43 pt 2 p.683). At 1 p.m. on 29 Nov Halleck asked Sheridan whether the report about Gordon's division should stop the detachment, since the President and Stanton thought it useless to send it at present: "Please answer immediately, as I have ordered steamers here" (p.695); at 2.30 p.m. Sheridan answered that it should go at once.' Replace 'E45 ... is very probably that steamer order' with 'E45 is plausibly one of the orders behind Halleck\'s "I have ordered steamers here" (inference).' what_is_added: replace 'Baltimore's steamers were called to Washington the morning of 29 Nov, before Sheridan confirmed the corps would leave' with 'The steamer order itself is in print through Halleck\'s remark; E45 adds only that Rucker called Baltimore\'s steamers and propellers to Washington at about 10.45-11 AM on 29 Nov.'

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Stanton via Capt. Bruch, Louisville, to Burbridge, 7 Aug 1864, hear Surgeon Ferry's statement and send him to Washington under guard (E68)
verdicts.reason: The whole Surgeon Ferry instruction is in clear in the public transcription (cached p9039.json). It reads: 'please see Surgeon Ferry in person & hear his statement ... If you deem his [communication] trust worthy & important send its substance by ___ ___ ... Send him here under adequate ___ that will take care he does not escape'. So the existence of the Ferry matter was not something the key revealed. The key adds Burbridge as recipient (the 'Burr' half is plain), 'cipher telegraph', 'guard' and the Secretary of War's signature. Ferry is unidentified. My Internet Archive full-text queries ('"Surgeon Ferry" 1864 Kentucky', '"Dr. Ferry" Burbridge 1864') found nothing relevant. Without knowing what Ferry said, this is a thread, not a fact, as the reader's own why_tier concedes. The reading is D3 (89%), with 'Jones' M and 'platation' I.
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: replace 'The existence of the Surgeon Ferry matter and Stanton's handling of it' with 'Little: the instruction about Surgeon Ferry (see him, hear his statement, forward it, or send him under guard so he does not escape) is in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9039); the key adds Burbridge as recipient, "cipher telegraph", "guard" and the Secretary of War's signature, i.e. that the order was Stanton's.' Context: keep 'the text does not say what the statement concerned' and drop any hint of a link to the conspiracy cases unless one is found.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: C. A. Dana to Baltimore, 5 Nov 1864 11 PM, Colonel William Hamilton reported as a Rebel agent in Baltimore (E96)
verdicts.reason: The substance is in print, and both audits missed it. James D. Horan, Confederate Agent (1954), p.226 (full text on Internet Archive as dli.ernet.157117, read this session) quotes Judge Advocate General Holt's report to Stanton on the informant Jones's disclosures. The report lists Rebel agents by city: 'Portland, Me. ... Major Dudley Harris ... Boston ... Col. J. D. Martin ... Baltimore ... Col. Wm. Hamilton ... Memphis ... Capt. Pope ... Cincinnati ... Maj. Heikermere ...'. This is the same list that put E29 at N2, and it matches the 5 Nov sibling orders to Cincinnati, New York and Memphis. So that Colonel William Hamilton was named as a Rebel agent at Baltimore is printed. The telegram adds only the order's date and its caution about the name. The audits' N3 (weak) should drop to N2, the E29 shape (for the parent to propagate to AUDIT.md, status.json and SO-ECKERT-E96; I edited nothing). The election and Camp Douglas framing in the context is not supported by anything in the telegram or the print. These orders carry out Jones's list. One real point does come out of the comparison: Horan dates the arrests to 24 Nov, after Holt's report of 23 Nov, while the ledger's clear sibling orders and E29 order arrests on Monday 7 Nov. That point rests on the clear pages and E29, not on E96.
verdicts.wording_fix: context: replace 'This was three days before the presidential election ... amid fears of plots against the election. E96 appears to be the Baltimore part of that sweep' with 'On 5 Nov 1864 Dana sent orders to arrest, on Monday 7 Nov, Rebel agents in New York, Cincinnati and Memphis; the names match the list of agents given by the informant Jones and summarized in Holt's report to Stanton (printed in Horan, Confederate Agent, 1954, pp.226-227), and E96 is the Baltimore entry of that list. Any link to the election or to the Camp Douglas arrests is not shown.' what_is_added: replace 'Per the audits, the 5 Nov arrest set is not in the Official Records' with 'Its substance is in print: Horan (1954) p.226 lists "Baltimore ... Col. Wm. Hamilton" among the agents Jones named. The telegram adds only the date of the order and its caution about several men of that name. Class should be N2 (content in print, no prior mapping of this ciphertext to it found), not N3.'

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Quartermaster General via Capt. Bruch to Brig. Gen. Allen, Louisville, 12 Dec 1864 2 PM, should the Military Railroads take the Louisville and Nashville (E146)
verdicts.reason: The reader already marked this 'provisional', and the default is to demote. More importantly, the public transcription (cached p9139.json) already shows the shape of the exchange in clear: 'Donaldson recommends that the manager of ___ States Military ___ be instructed to take immediate possession ...', 'Do you concur in his opinion', 'rolling stock', and the hesitation itself, 'Will not the ___ and ___ ___ company be able to do all that is possible and without the interruption caused by changing hands'. Meigs's preference is therefore not brought out by the key. The key supplies only which road (and Louisville, Army, the QMG signature), and with Allen at Louisville and Donaldson at Nashville the L&N was guessable. The proposal was not carried out. The reading is a weak N3 at D2, with 'Tartan' and 'Stan' unread and the closing sentence garbled. The L&N literature that would settle whether this is known is unread. That includes Dan Lee's 2011 book, whose stated subject is 'the struggle to control' the road. My two web searches and one Internet Archive full-text query found no discussion of Donaldson's December recommendation, and Google Books was at quota (HTTP 429). It stays useful-detail only on that provisional basis.
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: replace 'It also brings out Meigs's apparent preference to leave the company running' with 'The Quartermaster General's hesitation ("Will not the ... company be able to do all that is possible ... without the interruption caused by changing hands") is itself in clear in the public transcription; the key supplies the road (Louisville and Nashville Railroad), Louisville, Army and the Quartermaster General's signature.' why_tier: replace 'A historian of the L&N's wartime relations with the government, or of USMRR policy, would want to cite it' with 'It may interest a historian of the L&N's wartime relations with the government if Lee (2011), Klein (1972) or the QMG/USMRR records do not already discuss Donaldson's recommendation; the seizure was not carried out.' Name the sender as 'the Quartermaster General's office (signature = Qr Master Genl U.S.)' rather than Meigs in person.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: the Secretary of War to Dana, 6 June 1864, two French officers (N2-T)
verdicts.reason: The episode, including the ranks, is in print, and the officers can very probably be named. Theodore Lyman, Meade's Headquarters 1863-1865 (1922), p.178, letter of 25 June 1864 (Internet Archive meadesheadquarte00lyma, read this session), says: 'This morning appeared General Grant with two French officers ... two artillery officers, the elder a Colonel de Chanal, the other a Captain Guzman, both sent as a commission to observe the progress of the campaign'. That is a colonel and a captain, arriving a week after Grant's printed agreement of 18 June. Beauvais, Attachés militaires (1937; Internet Archive IA41552225_0063, snippet via full-text search) describes the 1864 mission of Lt-Col. de Chanal and Capt. Guzman, and a letter from the Secretary of War's aide preparing de Chanal for the army's privations. Dana's replies of 7 and 18 June print the topic and both of Grant's answers. V1-G3A already marked the N4 'weak' because most of the frame is public in clear. What remains ours is only the query's wording and the week's hold-up. The 'July 1864' date for Lyman in the context is wrong: the letter is 25 June.
verdicts.wording_fix: context: replace 'A Colonel de Chanal appears with Meade's staff in Theodore Lyman's letters of July 1864, so he may be the colonel here. That is plausible, not established.' with 'Lyman's letter of 25 June 1864 (Meade's Headquarters, 1922, p.178) records Grant arriving with "two artillery officers, the elder a Colonel de Chanal, the other a Captain Guzman, both sent as a commission to observe the progress of the campaign", so the telegram's colonel and captain are very probably de Chanal and Guzman (inference: the telegram names no one).' what_is_added: replace 'It adds the observers' ranks and the week's hold-up' (why_tier) with 'The ranks are in print (Lyman 1922); the query adds only Stanton's wording and the week's hold-up.' Keep the AUDIT's clause on the public clear words with any mention of N4.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Fry to Manierre (and to W. E. Dodge), 2 Nov 1864, withdraw as a candidate for Congress or resign (E37)
verdicts.reason: As a document it is interesting, but the reader's own admission decides the tier. The instruction, 'I advise the former', Fry's name and the copy to Dodge are all in clear in the Huntington's public volunteer transcription (cached p9110/p9111.json, which I confirmed). Our decipherment adds only Captain, the 8th District, New York, Washington, 'telegraphed' and General. The telegram states no motive. I grepped OR III/4 (cu31924079575373) for 'candidate' and found no Provost Marshal General rule on candidacies, which leaves a propriety reading and a partisan reading equally open. The outcome is in print (Manierre's letter of 2 Nov, NYT and Tribune 4 Nov; the Dodge vs. Brooks record). The class is N3, not N4. 'Notable' overstates both what is established and what is ours. The context facts are accurate: Manierre withdrew and backed Dodge, Brooks won the count, and Dodge was seated in 1866 after contesting it.
verdicts.wording_fix: why_tier: replace 'A historian of the 1864 election in New York, or of Democratic charges of military interference that year, would want to cite it' with 'A historian of the 1864 election in New York might cite it, but the instruction, Fry's signature and the copy to Dodge have been readable in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointers 9110-9111); our key fixed only the district, state and titles, and the telegram gives no motive.' context: replace 'Brooks's contest notice alleged' with 'Brooks's pleading in the Dodge vs. Brooks contested-election record alleged'. Outward wording must carry AUD2-LS-C's added clause ('Manierre's withdrawal itself was printed on 4 Nov 1864, without the instruction'), must say the clear words are public, and must avoid 'secret order that forced Manierre out'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: F. W. Seward to C. A. Seward, 15 Oct 1864, Havana consuls, Hunter and Tassara; see Evarts (E41)
verdicts.reason: On its face this is a list of names and posts plus a request to see Evarts. All of that is in clear in the public transcription (cached p9097.json). The key adds only 'General', 'Department', 'Washington' and the street number. The tie to the Argüelles affair is inferred: LS-V3 calls it 'plausibly that affair, inferred, not checked'. My web search confirmed the affair and the later prosecution 'The People vs. Robert Murray et al.' (Seward Project), but not Evarts's role or why the telegram was sent. Even if the link holds, it adds a small step to a known affair with no new fact. The context facts are accurate as far as checked: Murray's seizure of Argüelles at Spain's request without a treaty, Savage at Havana, and C. A. Seward as the Secretary's nephew.
verdicts.wording_fix: context: replace 'The names match the Arguelles affair.' with 'The names and titles match the officials in the printed Argüelles correspondence (Papers relating to Foreign Affairs, 1864); the telegram's purpose is not stated and the link is inferred.' why_tier: replace 'shows the State Department lining up the officials involved and seeking Evarts's help in the Arguelles litigation' with 'would show the State Department lining up officials and seeking Evarts's help, perhaps in the prosecution of Marshal Murray (inference)'. Outward wording should say the names and the request to see Evarts are public in clear in the Huntington transcription.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: to John A. Kennedy, New York police, 30 Nov 1864, suspected chief conspirator of the New York fires in the Old Capitol (E46)
verdicts.reason: The decipherment adds almost nothing. I read the cached Huntington transcription p9130. The whole message is in clear there: 'Mr Kennedy Supt Police ... A man believed toby the man described ... evening ... of Monday as being the chief conspirator forth burning of ... is ... old capital prison send on a man to identify him'. Kennedy's name and title already point to New York. The key adds only 'New York' (twice), 'Post' and 'in the'. The description the telegram cites is printed (Evening Star, 29 Nov 1864, quoting the Post; LS-V3). The suspect is unnamed, the signature is unread, and the 'false lead' reading is inference. It is a trace of the War Department's hunt, but that trace was already readable in the holder's public transcription. Web search (Wikipedia, Robert Cobb Kennedy) confirms the 25 Nov fires, his capture at Detroit and his hanging at Fort Lafayette on 25 Mar 1865. It gives no arrest date, so the reader's '29 Dec' is unconfirmed.
verdicts.wording_fix: Context: 'R. C. Kennedy was taken only at Detroit on 29 Dec' -> 'R. C. Kennedy was arrested at Detroit at the end of December 1864 (exact day not confirmed here)'. 'A man held in the Old Capitol on 30 Nov as the chief conspirator was therefore apparently a false lead' -> 'No record located shows that the man held in the Old Capitol on 30 Nov was one of the incendiaries, all of whom reached Canada by Headley's account; that he was a false lead is my inference.' what_is_added should open with: 'Nothing of substance: the message is in clear in the Huntington's public transcription (pointer 9130); the key supplies only New York, Post and in the.'

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: C. A. Dana to Wallace, Baltimore, 7 Nov 1864, a rebel agent calling himself Dr Hamilton (E52)
verdicts.reason: The manhunt is in clear on p9117 ('agent calling himself Dr Hay mill ton passed through Elmira on his way ... on Thursday last ... light hair must ache & whiskers & fine teeth ... catch him'). The key adds Rebel, South, the height, the sender (Insanity = Dana, H) and the addressee (Submit = Wallace, a C-grade key row derived from a May 1864 print). The historically interesting part is Dana's arrest orders of Saturday 5 Nov to Cincinnati, New York, Memphis and St Louis. Those are in clear in the same ledger and unprinted in OR II/7, I/43 pt 2 and I/41 pt 4 (AUDIT V1-LS4B), and they are not ours. The press pass for E52 is incomplete (7 of 15 pages read). The link to the 'Colonel William Hamilton' of E96 is inference. The result is a routine descriptive circular. I checked AUDIT LS-V4, AUD2-LS-E and V1-LS4B and the cached transcription. Lew Wallace commanding the Middle Department and Dana as Assistant Secretary of War are accurate.
verdicts.wording_fix: Context: 'It belongs to Dana's arrest orders of 5 Nov for rebel agents in several cities, to be carried out on Monday 7 Nov' -> 'It follows Dana's arrest orders of Saturday 5 Nov (in clear in the same ledger) for rebel agents in several cities, to be executed "on Monday morning next", 7 Nov.' 'The Camp Douglas conspirators in Chicago were seized the same night' -> 'Col. B. J. Sweet's arrests of the Camp Douglas plotters in Chicago fell in the early hours of the same Monday, 7 Nov (from general knowledge; not checked here).' what_is_added: 'the addressee (Wallace)' -> 'the addressee (Wallace, by a C-grade key row)'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Stanton to Maj. Gen. Peck, New York, 3 Sept 1864 8.30 PM, the plot to seize the Sound steamers passed to the Navy (E123)
verdicts.reason: This survives because the key, not the clear frame, carries the point. On p9062 the offer reads '... any service tooth owners or shippers whack saddling or niggarding their vessels'. Whack = Towards, Guard(-ing) and Niggard = Arms are all H, so the offer to help private owners guard or arm their steamers is the key's contribution. The Navy referral it decodes is independently confirmed: ORN I/3 p.197 prints Eckert forwarding Peck's telegram to Welles the same day at Stanton's direction. Peck's report is in OR I/43 pt 2 p.21. The reply was not located in OR, ORN, Welles's diary, IA full text or Google Books (FV-LS5-B, AUD2-LEDGER-2). Depth D3 (94.1%, 16 of 17 H, tail 'French' M).
