It remains a small addition to a printed episode, and the class is a weak N3.
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: 'the key adds telegram, rebel, steamers, Secretary of the Navy and the signature' -> 'the key adds telegram, rebel, steamers, communicated, Secretary of the Navy, Department, "towards guarding or arming" (the substance of the offer), inform, and the signature (Secretary of War)'. Context: 'This was one of the maritime plots from Confederate agents in Canada that autumn' -> 'Peck's report calls it a plot of "Confederate pirates"; nothing printed ties it to the Canada operatives, though their seizure of the Philo Parsons on Lake Erie followed on 19 Sept.' Caveat: 'The press of the day was unreachable' -> 'The New York press of 4-6 Sept 1864 is unread (one loc.gov timeout; the first audit did not search it); the plot itself was reported in the New York Herald of 3 Sept 1864 (cited in Spann, Gotham at War, per AUD2-LEDGER-2).'

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: General-in-Chief to Hunter, Cedar Creek, 22 May 1864 10.30 PM, not sent: no reinforcements without Grant's orders (E106)
verdicts.reason: The key does supply the substance (Weakness = Reinforcements, Quadroon = Department, Jupiter = Grant, Whisky/Whist = Troops, all H), and the text is not located in OR I/37 pt 1 or the Grant Papers snippets. But it is a draft that was struck out and never sent, and it restates the known May 1864 line that troops went where Grant ordered. Two replies that were sent are printed: E9 ('brigadiers are scarce') and Halleck's 9 p.m. note on vacancies (OR I/37 pt 1 p.525). The only point of real interest, that the clerk read Hunter's request for brigadiers as '2 brigades' and that this explains the withdrawal, is inference. The class is a weak N3 at D3 (81%), with Hunter C-grade and Cedar M. At most it is a curiosity for a footnote on the Lynchburg campaign. One factual error: in May 1864 Halleck was Chief of Staff (from 12 Mar 1864) and Grant was General-in-Chief. The signature code word Jonah = 'General-in-Chief' is the older key's row. I checked AUDIT FV-LS5-A and AUD2-LEDGER-1, cached p8969 and reading.md.
verdicts.wording_fix: Title: 'General-in-Chief to Hunter' -> 'Halleck's office to Hunter (signed with the key's "General-in-Chief" code word; by May 1864 Halleck was Chief of Staff and Grant General-in-Chief)'. Context: 'and was about to march on Lynchburg' -> 'and was about to advance up the Valley (he moved south in late May; Lynchburg came in mid-June)'. what_is_added: 'An unsent draft, located in no print' -> 'An unsent draft, not located in print (OR I/37 pt 1 read by date, Grant Papers vols 10-12 by snippet, IA full text, Google Books; 8 Oct 2026)'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864 (Fort Monroe ledger): Butler's HQ to Fort Monroe, 2 Nov 1864 2.30 PM, officers, men and guns of five batteries (E160)
verdicts.reason: The numbers are key-dependent (43 of 43 H after FV-FM1's corrections) and not located in print, but this is a routine strength return for a list of candidate batteries. The batteries actually sent and their guns are printed: Battery M, 1st U.S. and the 4th New Jersey, 'each of six light 12's' (OR I/42 pt 3 p.490; Hawley's report, I/43 pt 2 p.559; AUD2-LEDGER-3). The 4th New Jersey is not on the list. The only fact here that bears on what happened is Battery M's 3 officers and 110 men. The ledger also contradicts itself on the 17th New York's guns (3-inch in E162, Napoleons in E160). Purpose, composition and dates are all already in print. I checked AUDIT FV-FM1 and AUD2-LEDGER-3 and reading.md (which carries the corrected 'six 3-inch' readings).
verdicts.wording_fix: Content: 'Butler's chief of artillery gives Fort Monroe' -> 'Lt. Col. Howard, Butler's chief of artillery (through operator R. O'Brien), gives Fort Monroe'. Also 'the 17th New York, Napoleons, 4 officers and 166 men' -> 'the 17th New York (Napoleons here, 3-inch guns in the previous day's list, E162), 4 officers and 166 men'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Biggs, 19 Apr 1864, steamers chartered for Fort Monroe (E21)
verdicts.reason: I grepped the cached OR I/33 djvu. Wise's report of 19 Apr from Philadelphia (received 9 p.m., p.915) lists 17 side-wheel boats, 11 propellers, 8 steam-tugs and 50 canal barges, with 'comfortable transportation for 20,000 men'. Meigs's order to Wise of 16 Apr is also printed. E21, sent at 1 PM, gives lower counts (10/4/7/2/40) for Philadelphia and Baltimore. That is an earlier, partial tally, superseded the same evening by the printed fuller one, not a summary of it. The vessel names are in clear on p8934-8935. Three of the seven names (Matilda, Highland Light, Champion) are on Wise's printed Philadelphia list, so the telegram's list is not clearly Van Vliet's New York charters. What is left that is ours and unprinted: 3 ferry boats and 3 tugs from Washington, and the Warrior plus double-decked barges for 700 cattle. That is ordinary quartermaster traffic. The reading is solid (D4, 37/37 H).
verdicts.wording_fix: what_is_added: 'Wise's half summarises his own printed report' -> 'Wise's counts here (10 side-wheel, 4 propellers, 7 tugs, 2 steam barges, 40 canal barges, sent 1 PM) are an earlier, smaller tally than his printed Philadelphia report received at 9 PM the same day (17 side-wheel boats, 11 propellers, 8 tugs, 50 canal barges; OR I/33 p.915)'. Content: 'Maj. Van Vliet at New York has chartered steamers (George Leary, Helen Getty, Metamora, Champion, Matilda, Highland Light, Richland) and many schooners' -> 'Maj. Van Vliet at New York has chartered steamers and many schooners; among steamers already chartered (the telegram does not say by whom; Matilda, Highland Light and Champion are on Wise's printed Philadelphia list) are George Leary, Helen Getty, Metamora, Champion, Matilda, Highland Light and Richland'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Seward to Palfrey, Boston postmaster, 12 Aug 1864, seize Keith's remittance letter to N. Ferris (E38)
verdicts.reason: The substance is in clear on p9045, which I read: Keith, Halifax, St Johns, N. Ferris, Market St, Boston, Palfrey, 'very impt to the ... to get possession of that letter', 'forward to me ... State'. The key adds 'rebel', '10 North', Government, Department and the signature. The watch on Keith's mail is already attested in print (Bates prints the Dec 1863 interception) and by clear siblings in the ledger: p9042 of 11 Aug 1864 orders the watch, and pp.9816-9817 of 10-11 Aug carry 'catch Keith who purchased the locomotives'. Whether the letter was seized is unknown, and Ferris is unidentified. The Keith biography in the context (Halifax agent, Chesapeake affair, Bremerhaven 1875) is accurate per web search. But the decipherment adds little to what the holder's transcription already showed. N3, D3, 13/13 H; AUDIT LS-V3 and AUD2-LS-C checked.
verdicts.wording_fix: Context: 'Bates prints that US authorities had kept a watch on mail addressed to Keith since Dec 1863' -> 'Bates prints Keith letters intercepted in Dec 1863 by the New York postmaster Wakeman, "who had been instructed by the authorities to keep a sharp lookout for communications addressed to Keith"; a clear ledger sibling of 11 Aug 1864 (p9042) orders the watch again'. 'E38 belongs to a 12-14 Aug 1864 cluster' -> 'E38 belongs to a 10-14 Aug 1864 cluster'. Caveats sentence stands; add to the outward safe line: 'its clear words are public in the Huntington's transcription (pointer 9045)'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Meigs to Ingalls, City Point, 24 July 1864, cavalry horses and the money shortage checking deliveries (N2-BI)
verdicts.reason: This survives because the key supplies what the clear clause is about and the hard numbers. 'Silvers' = Horse, Pedlar = Cavalry and Pagan = Artillery are H in key-no2, as are the figures: about 1,000 cavalry horses on hand and 3,962 issued at Washington from 1 to 24 July (Austin-Seward-Ellsworth-Yoke & Perkins-Arnold). They were not located in OR I/37 pt 2 or I/40 pt 3, nor in the Grant Papers vol. 11 (AUDIT LS-V6, AUD2-LS-G). It is the Quartermaster-General's own statement tying the money squeeze to remount supply, the kind of evidence Wilson (2006) uses. The reader's content leaves out that the telegram itself lists 'Invasion' (a plain word, not in key-no2) first among the causes. The reader's Early's-raid context should rest on that word, not on an unsourced claim that remounts were pulled to the capital. The 'rejoin' caveat is also slightly off: 'presume' is a plain word (the decoder's 'Hotly [?]' is an artefact) and 'ree [Join]' rests on Sweden = Join, H. Depth D2 (96.7%).
verdicts.wording_fix: Content: 'Depreciation of vouchers and certificates and a short supply of money have lately checked deliveries of horses' -> '"Invasion", depreciation of vouchers and certificates and a short supply of money have lately checked deliveries of horses'. Context: 'Early's raid on Washington (11-12 July) had pulled troops and remounts to the capital. At the same time the Union Treasury was short of cash after Chase's resignation on 30 June, so quartermaster vouchers traded at a discount' -> 'The telegram's own clear word "Invasion" plausibly means Early's invasion of Maryland (9-14 July), which would have disrupted deliveries; that summer the Treasury was also short of currency (Chase's resignation was accepted on 30 June), and quartermaster vouchers and certificates traded at a discount'. Caveat: 'The rejoin token is uncertain (Hotly [?])' -> '"I presume" is plain (the decoder's "Hotly [?]" is an artefact); "rejoin" rests on Sweden = Join, H; one I-grade token'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: to Capt. G. D. Wise, New York, 20 Apr 1864, transports for Butler's expedition (O9-AH)
verdicts.reason: The figures that make it interesting are all in clear on p8937, which I read: thirty thousand men, two thousand horses, 'of ten', one hundred wagons, 14,000 / 6,000 / 1,800, the 24th and 25th, and 'room to lie down ... fresh for their mornings work'. The key adds Butler's name (obvious from context), Fort Monroe and the nouns. The reading is D2 and the sender is not in clear. A second error came to light: the context, and the AUD2-LS-G audit line it copies, call the 16 Apr order to Wise 'Halleck's'. In the cached OR I/33 text it is signed 'M. C. MEIGS, Quartermaster-General' (5 p.m., 16 Apr). The 24th/25th deadlines also match Grant's 16 Apr letter to Butler ('impossible to move earlier than the 25th, so I will set that date for making your calculations', OR I/33 pp.885-886) better than his 18 Apr letter (no earlier than the 27th). A nice detail, but one already readable without the key.
verdicts.wording_fix: Context: 'Halleck's 16 Apr order sending Wise to Philadelphia and New York' -> 'Meigs's order of 16 Apr, 5 p.m., sending Wise to Philadelphia and New York to consult Crosman and Van Vliet (OR I/33, signed M. C. Meigs; AUD2-LS-G's "Halleck" is not supported by the print)'. 'Grant's letter to Butler of 18 Apr (OR I/33) says the start could not be fixed earlier than the 27th, which fits the 24th/25th deadlines here' -> 'The 24th/25th deadlines match Grant's letter to Butler of 16 Apr ("impossible to move earlier than the 25th, so I will set that date for making your calculations", OR I/33 pp.885-886); on 18 Apr he put the earliest start at the 27th, and the move began on 4 May'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Augur to Sheridan, 21 Aug 1864 4 PM, 100 Spencer rifles and 20,000 rounds to Harpers Ferry (E122)
verdicts.reason: The quotable sentence is in clear on p9053, which I read: 'I doubt if a ... men are sufficient for the work they are undertaking', with 'Spencer rifles', 'rounds of ... for them will be sent you at once' and the signature Augur. Sheridan's request and the War Department's approval are printed (OR I/43 pt 1 p.860, confirmed by FV-LS5-A), and the Spencers' issue to Blazer's men is in secondary print (Stephenson 2001, per AUD2-LEDGER-1). The key adds only Sheridan, the numbers 100 / 20,000 / 100, 'ammunition' and Harpers Ferry. The class is a weak N3 at D3 (81.8%). The context also overclaims. Web search (Wikipedia 'Blazer's Scouts', NPS, the Shenandoah blog) shows Blazer's unit already existed: Crook had reorganized it in spring 1864. Sheridan's request armed it with Spencers; it did not originate it. Kabletown, 18 Nov 1864, is correct.
verdicts.wording_fix: Context: 'That request is the origin of Capt. Richard Blazer's Independent Scouts, armed with Spencers' -> 'That request is generally linked to the arming with Spencer rifles of Richard Blazer's Independent Scouts, a unit Crook had reorganized in spring 1864'. what_is_added: add 'the request, its approval and the Spencers' issue to Blazer's men are already in print; the doubt sentence was legible in the Huntington's public transcription without the key'.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: G. V. Fox to Olcott, 2 May 1864, investigate the New York Navy Yard only, not prosecute (E23)
verdicts.reason: The substance is already readable and already in print. Only 7 code words are enciphered. The rest of the body is in clear in the Huntington's public transcription; I read p8955.json on disk: 'Do not proceed against anyone in Frog Yard ... investigate only not to prosecute ... That will be done by the Burton ...'. So the key adds only 'New York' and 'Secretary of the Navy'. The policy the telegram carries is also printed in Welles's diary, vol. 2 (IA full text diaryofgideonwel02welluoft, checked 8 Oct 2026). On 2 Apr 1864: 'Cautioned Fox to beware of yielding to the suggestions and opinions of detective Olcott ... nothing be done in the way of seizure and arrest but by Mr. Wilson's direction'. On 13 Apr Eames is sent to Boston 'to supervise Olcott, who is fierce in diving into matters and often ... without judgment'. On 21 Apr Wilson has 'charges and specifications against the parties in New York' with the copyists. LS-V1 searched that diary only for E23's exact phrases, so this match on substance was never logged. E23 is one routine instance of a policy already in print. The N3 for the telegram's own text is unaffected. The rest of the context is accurate: Olcott, Whiting as the War Department's solicitor, Fox's letter of 18 Feb 1864.
verdicts.wording_fix: Replace 'The telegram shows the Navy Department keeping prosecution decisions with Welles early in Olcott's inquiry' with: 'The restraint is already on record: on 2 April 1864 Welles cautioned Fox against "detective Olcott" and ruled that nothing be done "in the way of seizure and arrest but by Mr. Wilson's direction" (Diary of Gideon Welles, vol. 2). The telegram applies that policy to the New York yard.' In why_tier, drop 'a real glimpse of the limits placed on a controversial fraud investigator' as a claim for this telegram, because Welles prints those limits.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Seward to Wakeman, New York postmaster, 12 Aug 1864, three Keith remittances to be seized (E39)
verdicts.reason: Demoted because the key adds very little. I read the public transcription (p9045.json). It already shows, in clear: Wakeman as addressee, Alex Keith Jr at Halifax 'via St Johns', N. Ferris '... Mkt St Boston', J. B. Hunter & Co, Gordon Bruce & Co, 'ship immy to Mitchell Kenner & Co Montreal', 'should at all hazards be secured & forwarded to me', 'This wrangle will be your authority', and the signature word 'Byron'. The sibling 9820 (13 Aug, to Marshal Murray: Gordon Bruce & Co are supplying machinery for Keith, to be shipped to Mitchell Kenner & Co) is also clear in transcription (AUD2-LS-C). The New York post office's standing watch on Keith's mail is in print (Bates, per LS-V3). The decode adds the sender's office (Secretary of State, by code word), 'New York', the street number and 'report to the Postmaster General'. It is not known whether any letters were seized or what they held. A Keith specialist could use the names, but those were already public. For what our decode adds, this is routine. The context is otherwise right: Keith, the Chesapeake affair, and Bremerhaven 1875 via Larabee as cited in the audit.
verdicts.wording_fix: Replace 'Wakeman had already intercepted Keith's cipher mail in Dec 1863; those are the letters the War Department telegraph office decrypted, as Bates recounts' with: 'In December 1863 the New York post office, told to watch for letters addressed to Keith, had intercepted cipher letters that the War Department telegraph office deciphered (Bates, Lincoln in the Telegraph Office).' Replace 'show a coordinated State, War and Post Office effort against his purchasing network' with: 'show State, War and Post Office telegrams aimed at Keith's purchases in the same week (the siblings are volunteer transcriptions, not decoded here).'

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Secretary of War to Dana, 4 June 1864, Lt Col Wade, the Senator's son, for Sheridan's staff (N2-BJ)
verdicts.reason: This is the closest call among the Eckert items. Two audits located no printed text. The cipher hides nearly all the meaning: the transcription shows only 'Wade Son ... Senator ... pluck & gal aunt try'. The context is accurate: Dana's role, Cold Harbor on 3 June, James F. Wade per Heitman, Senator Wade's committee, and the Wade-Davis bill, which passed Congress on 2 July 1864. But it is a staff-appointment enquiry, the most ordinary kind of War Department traffic. Its interest rests entirely on the father's name. It records a request, not an outcome, and Heitman puts Wade in the 6th U.S. Colored Cavalry (colonel from 19 Sept 1864), which suggests nothing came of it. It changes no account of Stanton, Wade or Sheridan. I was unsure, so per the brief I defaulted to routine. A biographer of James F. Wade could still cite it as an anecdote.
verdicts.wording_fix: Replace 'Stanton personally using Dana' with 'the Secretary of War (signed by code word) asking Dana'. In why_tier, add that the outcome is unknown and that Heitman shows Wade staying in colored cavalry service.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Capt. Geo. K. Leet to Lt. Col. Bowers, 14 Aug 1864, Sharpe's men and W. J. Lee's offered ride to Gordonsville (N2-BZ part 2)
verdicts.reason: About half the body, including the parts that make it interesting, is already in clear in the public transcription; I read p9047.json. It has: 'a man named W - J - Lee formerly employed by ... Sharpe offers to make a trip to ... on ... back starting ... morning if furnished with ... and ... dollars' and '... represent him to be a good & reliable man'. The key adds Gordonsville, horse, the weekdays, 'information', 'tomorrow' and the sum. It records an offer, not a result, and whether Lee went is unknown. The N3 is weak: the Grant Papers vol. 11 note for 14 Aug was seen only in snippets, so it could still fall. One token is M: 'Black', read as Cairo, which cannot be where Bowers was. This is routine Bureau of Military Information traffic. The context checks out: Anderson's detachment with Kershaw's division and Fitz Lee's cavalry, and the Grant Papers note dating Bowers's request to 10 Aug (AUD2-LEDGER-2).
verdicts.wording_fix: After 'That request is printed in a note of the Grant Papers vol. 11', add: 'Leet's 12 Aug telegram (E145) is the explicit answer to it ("your dispatch of the 10th"); that this 14 Aug message also answers it is not established.' Otherwise none.

verdicts.title: Eckert 1864: Capt. Geo. K. Leet to Lt. Col. Bowers, City Point, copy to Sheridan, 12 Aug 1864, Hill's brigade to Early, Fitz Lee at Orange C.H., Longstreet in the Valley (E145)
verdicts.reason: Knocked down on two counts. (1) The provenance angle is already in print. AUD2-LEDGER-2 records Sheridan to Halleck, Cedar Creek, 12 Aug 1864, midnight (OR I/43 pt 1 p.19): 'A telegram from Captain Leet and also one from General Max Weber locates Longstreet in the Valley'. So Leet is already named in print as a source of the Longstreet misreport, and Sheridan's 13 Aug reply to Grant (p.784) prints the Longstreet and Orange C.H. clauses. Leet's E120 (11 Aug, 'the whole Corps was moving to join Early') fits Sheridan's reference at least as well, so all E145 could add is which of Leet's telegrams. (2) The three clauses not in print are scout hearsay: Hill's brigade sent to Early, its division under marching orders, and the Central road not running beyond Beaver Dam. As far as I know the first is wrong; from general knowledge, Hill's corps stayed at Petersburg and fought at Globe Tavern on 18-21 Aug. The reading also has three M tokens, Shenandoah among them, and two unread words ('wolves', 'melds') in the very phrases that name the informants. Depth D2. This is a routine intelligence relay. The rest of the context is accurate: Anderson with Kershaw and Fitz Lee, Longstreet absent until October, Sheridan's withdrawal toward Halltown. Separately, the 8 Oct be-api check confirms that historians quote Sheridan's 13 Aug line.

verdicts.title: August of Saxony, cipher enclosure of 1561-64 (WVO 53, Nassau papers): read cryptanalytically, no key or sibling decipherment

Wahl (1891), pp.35-37 (IA full text, read 8 Oct 2026), prints that the Navarre question was live at the Saxon court that autumn. Imperial vice-chancellor Seld reported the Rhinegrave negotiating secretly with August as the King of Navarre's agent, and that 'Mos. de Bandoma' had sent August a gentleman. Goetz also cites the nuncio Delfino reporting on 2 Nov 1561 that August had gone far in promises to the King of Navarre. So August had his own Navarre channel, and Orange's added element is a single line of opinion. The reading is cryptanalytic (S 356, M 8), the key is ours, there is no external check of content, and the Collectie Japikse copy is unseen. This is routine news traffic. A historian of Orange's Saxon diplomacy might still quote the one-line judgement against Goetz's context.

verdicts.title: Elector August to Orange, Torgau 18 Nov 1561, cipher enclosure (WVO 57, KHA A 11/XIV B/41-6)
verdicts.reason: It holds, narrowly, after one correction. The event, its dates and August's reply are all in print. Goetz 1891 pp.35-36 (IA full text, read 8 Oct 2026) gives the second embassy to August: Joachim von Neuhaus and Vice-Chancellor Seld, instructed 1 Nov 1561. It also gives August's written answer of 16 Nov 1561, printed 'im Wortlaut' in Moser Nr. 17, a polite refusal to commit. So the reading does not date the embassy. What is ours is the channel: two days after answering the envoys without committing himself, August told Orange, Philip II's stadholder, in cipher and asked for secrecy. A specialist could use that, because Goetz p.42 n.1 prints Languet's report from Paris of 26 Oct 1561. It describes a rumour that Philip was sure of August, with 'die Verwandtschaft des Prinzen von Oranien' in play; Languet and Mordeisen dismissed it. The reading is strong (C 294 of 301, D3, period key from the contemporary decipherment of WVO 74). The caveat stands: August's Dresden minute with its 'Zettel' may carry the enclosure in clear.

verdicts.title: Gramont to Villandry, Rome, 20 May 1530 (BnF fr. 2980 f.29r)
verdicts.reason: This is a covering note. In the cipher Gramont tells the king's secretary to get a separate 'article' from the bearer. He says he showed 'someone' everything (probably the Pope, since 'nostre Sainct Pere ... instance' is read just before) so as to remove suspicion. The note never says what the business was. The why_tier admits this, and if the substance survives anywhere it is in f.30, which DV-AD3 lowered to D1 ('fragments read') on 8 Oct 2026. The words that make the item interesting are among the weakest. 'fondement' is decoded 'TONDEMENT'. NOTES.md calls some sign identifications in L01, L03-L07 and L13 probably wrong. The reading rests on one reconciled transcription, and only about two lines run as continuous French. Its D2 (93.8%) was set under the 4 Oct method and has not been re-ruled under the 8 Oct depth bar that dropped sibling f.30 to D1. At this length it would very likely drop too. Sending the core of a despatch as a separate piece under the secretary's cover, while showing the main despatch at court, is ordinary practice. Three statements in the context are wrong or overstated. Cambrai (Aug 1529) was nine months old and still awaiting execution, not 'just made'. The embassy ran from mid-1529 to late 1530, not April to June. The interceptions do not 'explain' the routing, because the letter gives its own reason. The what_is_added phrase 'content had never been printed' breaks rule 10. Checked: AUDIT.md sections 1, 3, 'N4 decision (final families)', 'Depth (DEPTH-REGRADE)', 'G3 check' and 'Depth re-rule (DV-AD3)', and reading.txt (568 tokens: H 532, S 1, M 30, U 5). No external lookup beyond the audit's own citations.
verdicts.wording_fix: context -> 'Gabriel de Gramont, bishop of Tarbes (created cardinal on 8 June 1530), was in Rome in spring 1530 on Francis I's Italian embassy, which ran from mid-1529 to late 1530. Florence was under imperial and papal siege. The same day Gramont sent the King an all-cipher letter (f.30, no.22; graded D1, fragments read) whose fragments mention la liberte de Florence and la ville et la force entre vos mains. The audit treats f.30 as the article apart only by inference. Imperial agents were taking French despatches at the time: Mai (26 May) reports Tarbes complaining that his courier had been stopped at Florence, and Loaysa (21 June) reports letters intercepted at Asti. But the letter gives its own reason for the separate article: to satisfy someone and remove suspicion.' what_is_added -> 'A partial reading, with Tomokiyo and Lasry's published Gramont 1530 key, of the cipher in a letter whose existence and date were already catalogued (BnF 1868; Catalogue des actes de Francois Ier IX). verdicts.title: Danzay to the Cardinal of Lorraine, dated 27 Jan 1557 (BnF fr. 20140 f.35-36)
verdicts.reason: The reading is fragmentary, and the one name that would give it political weight is shaky. The King of Denmark is named in the letter's clear opening ('Monseigneur, le Roy de Dannemarch continue...', AUDIT f.36r section). The cipher sign Tomokiyo keys as 'le Roy de Dannemarch' (LRD) reads as a plain r/R in V5, V11, V26 and V28 (NOTES.md key note 3, the 'a u q s b o u <LRD> g' = Augsbourg case). So the cipher 'mentions' of the King, which the why_tier and the depth sentence both lean on, are not secure. What remains is: someone 'a promis qu'ils s'en ploieroient volontiers' (subject unread), the chancellor 'peult beaucoup', 'les passions et affections de ceulx' whose help he needs, and a remittance-like phrase through Augsburg and the Lyon merchants 'avec le peu de perte pour le change'. The money sense is partly the solver's grade-I inference, and the f.35v/f.36r join is unread. No purpose, sum or party is stated, so this is routine resident's reporting and payment logistics. The content also misplaces Augsburg and the Lyon merchants on f.36r; they are at the foot of f.35v (V26-V28), and only the 'change' phrase is on f.36r. The H 546 of 705 includes 61 nulls on f.35, so 448 H signs carry text there. The context calls the Cardinal of Lorraine a man 'who with the Guises dominated' policy, but he was a Guise himself, and in January 1557 the Constable Montmorency was still the leading counsellor until Saint-Quentin. The Teulet quotation is slightly conflated: his index says the correspondence 'n'a pu etre retrouvee', and a note says only post-1567 letters were known. The 1550s phase is not undocumented either: the same volume holds sibling letters with contemporary decipherments (ff.16, 24, 30), from which Tomokiyo built the key. Checked: AUDIT.md sections 1, 'f.36r', 'N4 decision (Cryptiana closed)', 'Depth' and 'G3 check'; NOTES.md key notes; reading.txt and reading_f36.txt.
verdicts.wording_fix: content -> 'In fragments, Danzay's cipher mentions a promise that they would willingly employ themselves (a promis qu'ils s'en ploieroient volontiers; who promised is unread). It also mentions the chancellor, who peult beaucoup, and les passions et affections de ceulx whose help he needs. At the foot of f.35v it names Augsburg and les marchans de Lion, and f.36r opens avecques le peu de perte pour le change. The King of Denmark is named in the letter's clear opening. The cipher sign keyed as le Roy de Dannemarch reads as a plain r in several places, so its cipher occurrences are not secure mentions of the King.' context -> 'Charles de Danzay was the French resident in Denmark from 1548 to 1589. Here he writes from Copenhagen to Charles de Guise, Cardinal of Lorraine, one of Henri II's leading councillors; the Guises' ascendancy over the Constable Montmorency came only after Saint-Quentin (August 1557). The date may be 27 January 1558 new style, since French usage then often began the year at Easter. Either way it falls in the renewed war with Philip II after the truce of Vaucelles broke down, late in Christian III's reign. French crown borrowing ran through the Lyon money market, where German houses also lent, so a remittance through Augsburg and Lyon merchants is plausible, but that money sense is the solver's grade-I inference. Teulet (1851) wrote that Danzay's correspondence n'a pu etre retrouvee and knew only letters after 1567. The same BnF volume nevertheless holds sibling 1550s letters with contemporary decipherments (ff.16, 24, 30).' why_tier -> 'Fragments only: a promise of service, the Danish chancellor's influence, and what looks like a remittance through Augsburg and Lyon merchants. No purpose, sum or party is stated, and the cipher mentions of the King of Denmark are not secure.' what_is_added: change 'H 546 of 705' to 'H 546 of 705, of which 61 are nulls on f.35'.

verdicts.title: BnF fr.3251 no.86, Lodovico Birago to the Duke of Nevers, Saluzzo, 27 August 1572: the whole cipher read with Tomokiyo's published 1572 key
verdicts.reason: Most of what the why_tier credits to the cipher is already in the letter's clear text and in a sibling with a period decipherment. VERIFY-NEVBIR-86 notes that the clear prose on f.174r says Carmagnola's garrison is 'buona parte uganotti', and that it names 'il Baron de Sadres' on f.174r and again on f.176r. The 8 Sept 1572 letter no.87, whose contemporary clear decipherment is laid in with it (N0), also names the 'baron de Sadres' and ties Carmagnola's castle to 'la casa de Memoranci' (NOTES.md, the no.87 reading). So the 'Huguenot officers in the Carmagnola garrison' point needed no decipherment. The cipher's own additions are fragments with no plan, order or number: 'per le cose passate si rende odioso', 'pratica stretta' over the government, and 'la mala gratia d'altri'. The reading is cryptanalytic only (S 629, M 76, U 53 of 758; H 0, C 0), and the judge fails at -1.161 against real_p05 -0.905. 'Two captains' and 'remain troubled' are completions ('capita[ni]', 'trava[...]'). Its D2 was set on 4 Oct and has not been re-ruled under the 8 Oct depth bar. In the context, Carmagnola was a fortress of the French-held marquisate of Saluzzo. Savoy coveted it and seized it in 1588, but it was not Savoy's to 'want back'. My web searches did not independently confirm Birago's exact office; it rests on the audit's citation of Catherine de Medicis' Lettres IV. Checked: AUDIT.md 'no.86', 'Second audit', 'Depth' and 'Revision after audit' sections; NOTES.md NEVBIR-174V-A/B and the no.87 reading.

He says the baron de Sadres (des Adrets in the glossator\'s identification) per le cose passate si rende odioso. verdicts.title: Baluze 170 f.229r-v: Chavigny to d'Avaux, Amiens, 25 Aug 1640, bare cipher passage on the junction of the dukes' and the Landgravine's troops with Longueville
verdicts.reason: This is the strongest item of the five, but 'notable' outruns the evidence. First, the Eberstein clause and every other letter-sign word are grade M. All 180 letter signs are M, and AUD2 found them transcribed 'settled from context in this letter', so they are not independent of the reading. Only 29% of tokens are H, and the cipher clause of the depth bar is not met. In mitigation, a fluent clause producing the correct name of Melander's real successor is decent internal corroboration. Second, the command clause is largely clear text. 'A M DE LONGUEVILLE ET SOUBZ SON COMMANDEMENT MESMES QUAND' is in capitals in reading_b170f229.txt, so that part needed no key. Third, the background is in print. The 1640 junction quarrels and Eberstein's Hessian command are discussed in Noailles 1913 and Le Laboureur 1657, per AUD1. Deutsche Biographie (ADB/NDB on Eberstein, found by web search) states that Amalie Elisabeth gave him command of her troops in Melander's place in 1640. What remains ours is the coded intention to gratify Eberstein and the request that Salvius work on [73]. N3, not N4: the AAE Correspondance politique and the Hessian-side editions (Rommel VIII) are unchecked. Le Laboureur prints Chavigny's letters to Guebriant and was searched only for two phrases. My IA full-text query inside it for 'Eberstein gratification' found both words in the volume, but the gratification snippets name others, so the check is not decisive either way. Gratifying allied commanders was routine French subsidy practice, so the clause is a useful specific rather than a revealed policy. Two content errors also need fixing. The decode reads '...de creance pres de [73]', which means credit or standing with [73], not 'send credentials'. And Melander had resigned in 1640, not yet 'defected' (he took imperial service later). Checked: AUDIT.md (AUD1-B167, AUD2-B167); reading_b170f229.txt; WebSearch (Deutsche Biographie sfz14935, Wikipedia on Melander); IA be-api inside bub_gb_cM5KS3lziccC.

What may most displease [73] is that they want their troops joined to Longueville and under his command even when the two crowns\' armies are together (this clause is largely in clear text). If the Landgravine is put off by [73]\'s excessive firmness, nous perdrons les seuls adherents, and each will withdraw shamefully, laissant l\'ennemi maistre de la campagne. And on gratiffiera le comte d\'Heberstein qui luy doit succeder, to bind him to do better than his predecessor (the whole clause is in M-grade letter signs).' context: replace the Melander sentence with 'Peter Melander gave up the Hessian command in 1640 (he later served the Emperor).
